title: Callback interop
scopeHtml: Bridging callback, listener, Future and Rx APIs into suspend functions and Flow: suspendCoroutine vs suspendCancellableCoroutine, cancellation and double-resume rules, callbackFlow/channelFlow, awaitClose, library bridges, and how Retrofit does it.

notes.title: Bridging a callback to a coroutine
notes.html:
The idea. Old APIs say "call me back later": fetch(id, callback). Coroutines want to write val user = fetch(id) and just wait. A bridge turns "call me back" into "suspend until the callback happens".

Decision: suspend or Flow? Ask "how many results come from one call?"

  • Exactly one result (a network request, a permission result, a single location fix) -> suspend fun using suspendCancellableCoroutine.
  • Many results over time (location updates, sensor readings, a socket, Firebase listener) -> Flow using callbackFlow.
suspend fun Api.fetchUser(id: String): User = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    val call = fetch(id, object : Callback<User> {
        override fun onSuccess(u: User) = cont.resume(u)
        override fun onError(e: Throwable) = cont.resumeWithException(e)
    })
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel() }        // tell the SDK to stop
}

Checklist for every bridge: (1) resume exactly once, (2) map errors to exceptions, (3) cancel the underlying work when the coroutine is cancelled, (4) unregister listeners, (5) think about which thread the callback comes from.

Real-world. This is what Retrofit's suspend support, OkHttp Call.await() helpers, kotlinx-coroutines-play-services (Task.await()), CameraX/Media3 ListenableFuture.await() and Fused Location wrappers all do under the hood.

Everyday analogy. Ordering at a pizza shop. The callback style is "give us your phone number, we'll ring you"; the suspend style is "wait on the bench until your name is called, and leave if you change your mind".

Common interview traps.

  • Using a Flow for a one-shot result (or a suspend function for a stream).
  • Forgetting to cancel the SDK's work on coroutine cancellation.
  • Resuming with a mutable result that the SDK reuses later.

notes.title: suspendCoroutine versus suspendCancellableCoroutine
notes.html:
The idea. Both suspend the coroutine and give you a continuation to resume later. Only suspendCancellableCoroutine knows about cancellation.

The mechanism.

  • suspendCoroutine { cont -> ... }: the continuation is not cancellable. If the coroutine's Job is cancelled while waiting, the coroutine keeps waiting until you resume it, and the underlying work keeps running. Cancellation can appear to "hang".
  • suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont: CancellableContinuation<T> -> ... }: if the Job is cancelled, the coroutine resumes immediately with CancellationException, and your invokeOnCancellation handler runs so you can stop the work. A late resume is silently ignored.

Use suspendCancellableCoroutine by default; suspendCoroutine is only fine for operations that are truly instant. There is also suspendCancellableCoroutine internals: it returns a CancellableContinuationImpl with an atomic state (Active, CancelledContinuation, completed value), and resume is a CAS on that state.

Real-world. A KYC or camera-permission screen wrapped with suspendCoroutine kept collecting after the user left the screen, holding the Activity in memory; LeakCanary showed the Activity retained via the SDK's callback.

Everyday analogy. A waiting-room: suspendCoroutine makes you sit until called even if you decide to leave; suspendCancellableCoroutine lets you walk out and the receptionist cancels the appointment.

Common interview traps.

  • Using suspendCoroutine for network calls (not cancellable).
  • Thinking a late resume after cancellation throws (it is ignored for the cancellable version).
  • Confusing it with withTimeout, which relies on this cancellability.

notes.title: invokeOnCancellation and cleanup
notes.html:
The idea. invokeOnCancellation { } is your "cancel button" hook: when the coroutine is cancelled, run this to stop the real work (cancel the HTTP call, unregister the listener).

The mechanism and rules.

  • Registered on the CancellableContinuation; runs only if the continuation is cancelled, not on normal completion.
  • Runs synchronously on the thread that cancelled, so keep it fast, non-blocking and non-suspending, and make it thread-safe and idempotent. It can also race with the callback thread.
  • It must not throw; exceptions are reported as CompletionHandlerException to the thread's uncaught handler.
  • Only one handler may be installed per continuation; a second registration throws IllegalStateException.
  • Register it as early as possible (right after starting the work), otherwise a cancel can slip between start and registration; if already cancelled, the handler is invoked immediately.

Scenario: non-cancellable bridge leak. A news app uses a custom OkHttp Call.await() written with suspendCoroutine. Users swipe quickly through 8 categories; each swipe cancels the old scope, but the HTTP requests continue to completion. Data use grew 38% per session and server QPS rose; the response was discarded. Fix: suspendCancellableCoroutine and cont.invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel() } (OkHttp's Call.cancel() is thread-safe). Result: cancelled requests are aborted mid-flight and bytes saved.

Real-world. Retrofit's own await() extension uses invokeOnCancellation { cancel() } for the same reason.

Everyday analogy. Cancelling a taxi: the app (coroutine) shows "cancelled" at once, but you must also tell the driver (the handler), or they still drive to your door.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing the handler runs after normal completion.
  • Doing blocking work (Thread.sleep, network) inside the handler.
  • Registering two handlers.
  • Assuming cancellation of the coroutine automatically cancels the SDK request.

notes.title: Resuming twice and resume semantics
notes.html:
The idea. A continuation is a one-shot return ticket. You may use it once. Some SDKs fire onSuccess and then also onFailure or call onSuccess twice.

The mechanism.

  • resume twice on suspendCoroutine/suspendCancellableCoroutine: the second call throws IllegalStateException("Already resumed, but proposed with update ..."). If it is thrown on the SDK's callback thread (which has no handler), the app crashes there; Crashlytics shows it on a thread named like "sdk-callback-1" and 100% on the screen that uses that SDK.
  • Resume after cancellation: for CancellableContinuation, the resume is ignored (no exception). If the value is a resource (a Closeable), use resume(value) { cause -> value.close() } (the onCancellation overload) to release it.
  • Resume after resume but before the dispatcher runs the coroutine: the first resume wins; the state is already completed. A second resume still throws IllegalStateException, even though the coroutine has not run yet. If the coroutine is cancelled in that tiny window, the result is dropped.

Defensive fix (when you don't trust the SDK). Guard with an atomic flag, or check cont.isActive:

override fun onResult(r: Result) { if (cont.isActive) cont.resume(r) }

isActive is a check-then-act, so two threads could still race; for genuinely concurrent callbacks use AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) or tryResume-style handling. Prefer fixing/guarding at the bridge rather than catching the exception: catching hides the real SDK bug, and logging it (once) tells you about it.

Scenario. A KYC SDK's onComplete fired twice after a rotation (a vendor bug). Crashlytics: IllegalStateException: Already resumed on the SDK thread, 0.35% sessions. Fix: single-resume guard in the bridge plus a vendor ticket.

Everyday analogy. A cinema ticket scanned once: the second scan beeps red.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking the second resume is silently ignored (it throws, except after cancellation).
  • Using try/catch around resume instead of guarding.
  • Forgetting the onCancellation overload when the value must be closed.

notes.title: callbackFlow channelFlow and flow
notes.html:
The idea. All three build a Flow, but differ in who may emit and from where.

Builder Emit from Use for
flow { } only the collector's coroutine, sequentially pure suspending sequences
channelFlow { } any coroutine / any child, via send concurrent producers (parallel fetch, merge)
callbackFlow { } callbacks on any thread via trySend registering a listener; must call awaitClose

Why emit from a callback in flow { } fails. flow {} is context-preserving and checks it at each emit. Calling emit from a different coroutine/thread throws IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated: Flow was collected in [..], but emission happened in [..]. A callback is not a suspend context at all, so you cannot even call emit (suspend) there. callbackFlow/channelFlow put a Channel between the callback and the collector: trySend is non-suspending and thread-safe, and the collector receives from the channel.

fun Context.locationUpdates(): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
    val cb = object : LocationCallback() {
        override fun onLocationResult(r: LocationResult) { trySend(r.lastLocation!!) }
    }
    client.requestLocationUpdates(req, cb, Looper.getMainLooper())
    awaitClose { client.removeLocationUpdates(cb) }
}

Review of a location wrapper: it must remove the callback in awaitClose, choose a buffer (see buffer policy section) and request updates with a sensible interval; otherwise the GPS stays on after the screen closes, draining battery for drivers (Uber/Ola-type apps are especially sensitive).

Everyday analogy. flow {} is one cook cooking dishes and bringing each to the table. callbackFlow is a doorbell: whoever presses it from outside drops a note in a mailbox, and the waiter reads the mailbox.

Common interview traps.

  • Using flow {} plus launch { emit() }.
  • Using callbackFlow without awaitClose.
  • Using channelFlow when a plain flow is enough (extra buffering and complexity).

notes.title: awaitClose and leaks
notes.html:
The idea. The callbackFlow block must stay alive as long as the listener is registered. awaitClose { } suspends the block until the flow is closed or cancelled, and then runs your cleanup.

The mechanism. awaitClose(block) is roughly try { suspendCancellableCoroutine<Unit> { cont -> invokeOnClose { cont.resume(Unit) } } } finally { block() }. It returns when the channel is closed (by close(), cancel, or the collector being cancelled). The lambda is your unregister code. If you omit awaitClose, the block returns immediately, the underlying channel is closed, and callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block (a guard added so you notice the leak). The crash occurs in debug and release alike because the check is in the library, independent of R8.

fun batteryLevel(ctx: Context): Flow<Int> = callbackFlow {
    val r = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
        override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) { trySend(i.getIntExtra("level", -1)) }
    }
    ctx.registerReceiver(r, IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED))
    awaitClose { ctx.unregisterReceiver(r) }       // without this: crash, and leak if it didn't crash
}

You can also call close(error) from the callback to terminate the flow when the source is finished; awaitClose will then complete and run the cleanup.

Everyday analogy. Hanging a "Do not disturb" sign on a hotel door and removing it when you check out. awaitClose is the checkout step.

Common interview traps.

  • Omitting awaitClose (crash) or putting cleanup after it where it may not run when cancelled (use the lambda, which is finally).
  • Doing blocking cleanup inside awaitClose.
  • Thinking awaitClose waits for the callbacks to finish (it waits for close/cancel).

notes.title: Play services Task await
notes.html:
The idea. Firebase and Google Play services return Task<T> (like a Future with listeners). The artifact kotlinx-coroutines-play-services gives Task<T>.await().

Behaviour.

  • Success: returns the result.
  • Failure: throws the task's exception.
  • The task itself cancelled: throws CancellationException.
  • Coroutine cancelled: await() stops waiting and throws CancellationException, but does not cancel the Task itself unless you use the overload that takes a CancellationTokenSource (for tasks that support tokens, such as getCurrentLocation), where cancelling the coroutine also cancels the token (confirm with your library version). Most Firebase tasks (e.g. auth.signIn, Firestore writes) cannot be cancelled, so work may still happen.
  • A Task<Void> returns null as the result; mind nullability for Task<T?>.
  • Listeners are attached on an internal executor, not the Main looper; do not assume a thread.
val user = auth.signInWithEmailAndPassword(e, p).await().user

Real-world. Firebase Auth, Remote Config fetch, FCM token (FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().token.await()), Fused Location getCurrentLocation.

Everyday analogy. Leaving the queue at a bank counter does not make the teller stop processing your already-submitted form.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing coroutine cancellation cancels a Firebase write.
  • Forgetting that Task<Void>.await() returns null.
  • Not wrapping await() in try/catch for FirebaseException.

notes.title: ListenableFuture and CompletableFuture
notes.html:
The idea. CameraX, Media3, WorkManager (getWorkInfos), Play Billing helpers use Guava ListenableFuture; Java 8 code uses CompletableFuture. Both have coroutine bridges.

The mechanism.

  • kotlinx-coroutines-guava: ListenableFuture<T>.await(); future { } builds a ListenableFuture from a coroutine; asListenableFuture() for a Deferred.
  • kotlinx-coroutines-jdk8: CompletionStage<T>.await(), CompletableFuture, future { }, Deferred.asCompletableFuture().
  • Direction 1: cancelling the awaiting coroutine cancels the future (future.cancel(false)), propagating cancellation to the underlying work when the library supports it.
  • Direction 2: cancelling the future (someone calls future.cancel) makes await() throw CancellationException. When the future is created by future { }, cancelling it cancels the coroutine.
  • If the future fails, await() throws the cause (unwrapped from ExecutionException).
  • AndroidX has also ListenableFuture.await() in androidx.concurrent:concurrent-futures-ktx (confirm which artifact you use). Never use future.get() on the main thread: it blocks the UI and risks an ANR.

Everyday analogy. A tracking number: if you cancel the order the shop is told; if the shop cancels, you are told.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling .get() on Main.
  • Assuming a failure arrives wrapped (ExecutionException) when await() unwraps it.
  • Mixing up which artifact provides which await.

notes.title: Firebase listeners and sensors
notes.html:
The idea. Both are "register, receive many, unregister", so both fit callbackFlow with awaitClose.

fun DocumentReference.snapshots(): Flow<DocumentSnapshot> = callbackFlow {
    val reg = addSnapshotListener { snap, err ->
        if (err != null) { close(err); return@addSnapshotListener }
        if (snap != null) trySend(snap)
    }
    awaitClose { reg.remove() }
}

fun SensorManager.accel(): Flow<FloatArray> = callbackFlow {
    val l = object : SensorEventListener {
        override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) { trySend(e.values.clone()) }
        override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) {}
    }
    registerListener(l, getDefaultSensor(Sensor.TYPE_ACCELEROMETER), SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_UI)
    awaitClose { unregisterListener(l) }
}.conflate()

Differences: Firebase emits snapshots (cache first, then server) and errors, which end the listener (so close(err)). Sensors emit continuously at a rate set by you and never error. Sensor values arrays are reused by the framework, so clone() before sending. Choose rates sensibly: SENSOR_DELAY_FASTEST can emit hundreds of events per second and drain the battery; a conflate()d buffer fits "latest value" UIs.

Scenario: notification sounds 2, 3, then 5 times. A screen collects an SDK stream with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED). Each STARTED re-collects the cold callbackFlow, which registers a new SDK listener; the old registration was never removed because the SDK registers into a list and the code lacked awaitClose { unregister } or used a different (new) lambda instance for removal. After n re-starts there are n listeners, so each event is handled n times. Fix: unregister with the same listener instance in awaitClose, or make the SDK listener single-registration; verify by counting listeners in a debug log.

Everyday analogy. Subscribing to a newsletter every time you open the app but never unsubscribing: you get five copies of each email.

Common interview traps.

  • Registering a listener per collection without removing it.
  • Forgetting clone() on sensor arrays.
  • Not turning listener errors into close(cause).

notes.title: Retrofit suspend support
notes.html:
The idea. Retrofit 2.6 added support for suspend fun. You write suspend fun getUser(): User; Retrofit does the callback bridge for you.

The mechanism. At runtime Retrofit sees the extra Continuation parameter of the suspend method (the Kotlin compiler turns suspend fun f(): User into f(Continuation<User>): Any?). It builds the Call and uses an internal extension (KotlinExtensions.await) that is a suspendCancellableCoroutine:

suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }          // cancels the OkHttp call
    enqueue(object : Callback<T> {
        override fun onResponse(call: Call<T>, response: Response<T>) {
            if (response.isSuccessful) cont.resume(response.body()!!)   // null body -> KotlinNullPointerException
            else cont.resumeWithException(HttpException(response))
        }
        override fun onFailure(call: Call<T>, t: Throwable) = cont.resumeWithException(t)
    })
}

So HTTP errors (4xx/5xx) throw HttpException; network problems throw IOException; return Response<T> if you want to inspect the status yourself. Cancellation: cancelling the coroutine calls Call.cancel(), aborting the OkHttp request (the socket is closed, bytes stop). The call runs on OkHttp's own dispatcher (not blocking the caller thread), so no Dispatchers.IO is needed. The callback resumes on an OkHttp thread and the dispatcher moves the coroutine back to its own context.

Real-world. Almost every Android app (Swiggy, Paytm and so on) uses Retrofit+coroutines; catch HttpException and IOException separately and rethrow CancellationException.

Everyday analogy. Ordering delivery: leaving the app tells the restaurant to cancel the rider.

Common interview traps.

  • Wrapping calls in try { } catch (e: Exception) and swallowing CancellationException.
  • Declaring a non-null return for an API that may return empty body (204); use Response<Unit> or Unit.
  • Wrapping Retrofit suspend functions in withContext(IO) (unneeded).

notes.title: RxJava bridges
notes.html:
The idea. While migrating from RxJava to coroutines, kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 (also rx2) converts between the two worlds.

API. Rx -> coroutines: Single.await(), Maybe.awaitSingleOrNull(), Completable.await(), Observable.asFlow() / awaitFirst(). Coroutines -> Rx: rxSingle { }, rxCompletable { }, rxObservable { send(x) }, Flow.asObservable() / asFlowable().

What to reason about at each boundary.

  • Cancellation: disposing the Rx subscription cancels the coroutine; cancelling the coroutine disposes the Rx subscription (good; check each helper).
  • Back-pressure: Rx Flowable has back-pressure strategies; Rx Observable does not. Observable.asFlow() buffers (unbounded by default), so a fast Observable can balloon memory; add .buffer(n) / .conflate() explicitly. A Flow is naturally back-pressured by suspension.
  • Nulls: Rx 2/3 forbids null; Kotlin Flow allows it. Emitting null from rxObservable throws NullPointerException.
  • Errors: an onError becomes an exception from await()/collect; a thrown exception inside rxSingle { } is delivered to onError; exceptions after dispose go to RxJavaPlugins.onError (can crash the app if no global handler is set).
  • Threads: Rx subscribeOn/observeOn don't map to flowOn/dispatchers one-for-one; pick the context at the boundary.
  • Single vs suspend; Observable vs Flow; Completable vs suspend Unit mapping for incremental migration.

Real-world. Large apps (Uber, Netflix, Airbnb) migrated module by module, with a thin adapter layer so Rx and coroutines co-exist.

Everyday analogy. An electrical plug adapter between two countries; it passes power but each side keeps its own rules.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming asFlow() applies back-pressure to an Observable.
  • Forgetting that Rx cannot carry nulls.
  • Losing errors after disposal when no RxJavaPlugins.setErrorHandler exists.

notes.title: Callback threading and buffer policy
notes.html:
The idea. The SDK calls you from some thread at some speed. Your job is to hand values into the flow without blocking that thread and without growing memory.

Choosing the send function. Inside the callback (non-suspending):

  • trySend(x): returns immediately; if the buffer is full the value is dropped (or follows the overflow policy). Default for callbacks.
  • trySendBlocking(x): blocks the callback thread until there is room. Use only when losing a value is unacceptable and that thread is allowed to block (never Main).
  • send(x): suspend; only legal inside a coroutine (e.g. launch { send(x) } from the callback, which has its own ordering issues).

Choosing the buffer. callbackFlow defaults to Channel.BUFFERED (64). Use .buffer(n) / .conflate() after it or buffer(capacity, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST):

  • Latest-wins (location, sensors, battery): conflate() or DROP_OLDEST.
  • Every event matters (chat messages, payment status): a larger bounded buffer, and if overflow is possible, a design that persists them (database) rather than keeping them in memory. UNLIMITED only with a provably bounded source.

What can you lose? Dropped values under overflow; values emitted after the collector is cancelled; values while no collector is active (the cold callbackFlow registers only during collection, so events before collection are missed, unless the source replays). Document it.

Everyday analogy. A mailbox: if the box is full the postman either leaves the letter on the step (blocking), takes the oldest out (drop oldest) or walks away (drop latest).

Common interview traps.

  • Using trySendBlocking on the main thread.
  • Ignoring the trySend result.
  • Assuming events during the gap before collection are queued.

notes.title: Error mapping in bridges
notes.html:
The idea. Each failure should end up in the place the consumer expects: as an exception from a suspend function, or as a terminal error in a Flow.

Mechanism Used in Effect
resumeWithException(e) suspend bridge await() throws e
close(cause) callbackFlow/channelFlow flow completes with cause, collector's catch sees it
cancel(CancellationException(...)) channel/flow normal cancellation, not an error; treated as the end silently
throw inside callback SDK's thread usually crashes the app on that thread; not reported to the coroutine
throw from registration call inside callbackFlow block propagates as flow failure to the collector

Guidelines: use close(cause) for real errors; use close() (no cause) for "finished normally"; use CancellationException only for cancellation, never for domain errors; never throw from callbacks, translate to resumeWithException/close. In a stream, a recoverable error (a failed read) can be sent as a value (sealed Result) so the stream continues; terminal errors use close(cause). Wrap the registration (requestLocationUpdates) in try/catch for SecurityException and close the flow with it, otherwise it propagates correctly anyway but record it.

Everyday analogy. Reporting a problem: either a formal complaint that ends the contract (close(cause)), or a note in the daily log while work continues (error as a value).

Common interview traps.

  • Throwing CancellationException for domain errors (it will be swallowed as cancellation).
  • Throwing in SDK callbacks.
  • Mixing up close(cause) (terminal with error) and cancel (silent cancellation).

notes.title: Stateful and single-listener SDKs
notes.html:
The idea. Some SDKs have rules: one listener at a time, a required connection order, a single stream active at once. Mapping them to Flow means managing shared state carefully.

Single-listener API (setListener(l) replaces the old one). Three features want the network state. If each wraps setListener in its own callbackFlow, the last collector silently steals events from the others, and when one cancels, setListener(null) kills the rest. Solution: wrap the SDK once in a callbackFlow and share it with shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), replay = 1) (or stateIn). Then only one listener registration exists, started with the first subscriber and stopped after the last (plus a grace period).

Stateful device SDK (BLE glucose meter): connect, readHistory, startLiveStream, disconnect, with rules such as "no readHistory while streaming". Design:

  • Model a connection state machine (Disconnected -> Connecting -> Connected -> Streaming) as a StateFlow.
  • connect and readHistory as suspend functions (one result each) with suspendCancellableCoroutine; startLiveStream as a callbackFlow with awaitClose { stopStream() }.
  • Serialize commands through a Mutex or a single-consumer channel (actor) so rules cannot be violated by two coroutines.
  • Cancellation must map to SDK abort calls; disconnect() must be idempotent and called in finally/NonCancellable.
  • Own the SDK instance in a long-lived scope, not a screen's scope.

Real-world. Wearable apps (Fitbit/Garmin-style) use exactly this: state machine, one command queue, shared stream.

Everyday analogy. A single walkie-talkie channel: if two people each tune in and then one switches off, the other hears nothing; you need one operator who relays to everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • Creating one callbackFlow per consumer for a single-listener SDK.
  • Not using WhileSubscribed and leaving the listener registered forever.
  • Skipping command serialization for a stateful device.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• One result -> suspendCancellableCoroutine; many -> callbackFlow + awaitClose.
  • Always prefer the cancellable version and register invokeOnCancellation to stop the real work (fast, non-throwing, thread-safe).
  • Resume exactly once: double resume throws IllegalStateException; resume after cancel is ignored; guard against buggy SDKs.
  • flow {} cannot be emitted from another coroutine; channelFlow allows concurrent send; callbackFlow bridges callbacks with trySend.
  • Omitting awaitClose crashes with an explicit message; put the unregister in its lambda; use the same listener instance.
  • Task.await() does not cancel the task; Guava/CompletableFuture bridges cancel both ways; never get() on Main.
  • Retrofit suspend: suspendCancellableCoroutine + Call.cancel(); HTTP error -> HttpException.
  • Rx bridges: mind back-pressure, nulls, error after dispose, cancellation.
  • Pick trySend vs trySendBlocking and the buffer by what you can afford to lose; map errors with close(cause) or resumeWithException.
  • Single-listener and stateful SDKs: wrap once, shareIn(WhileSubscribed), state machine and serialized commands.

questions.promptHtml: You have an SDK with fun fetch(id: String, cb: Callback<User>). Walk me through how you expose it to coroutine code, and how you decide between a suspend function and a Flow.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know the one-shot vs multi-shot split, which decides the whole API shape, and that you can write the bridge from memory.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "First I ask how many times the callback can fire. Exactly once, success or error, means a suspend function built on suspendCancellableCoroutine: I register the callback, resume the continuation in onSuccess, resumeWithException in onError, and cancel the underlying work in invokeOnCancellation. Many times, like location, sensors or listeners, means a Flow built with callbackFlow: trySend from the callback, close(error) on failure, and awaitClose { unregister } as the last line. If a library already ships an await() or asFlow() (Task, Rx, Guava), I use that instead of hand-rolling."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A callback API inverts control: you hand over a function and the library calls you later, possibly on another thread. A suspend function gives control back to the caller's flow: the coroutine is suspended, and when the result arrives it is resumed. The bridge is therefore "save the Continuation, resume it from the callback".

one-shot   callback fires 1x (result XOR error)      -> suspend fun   (suspendCancellableCoroutine)
multi-shot callback fires 0..N times, then maybe     -> Flow          (callbackFlow)
           completes/errors
already a  Task / ListenableFuture / CompletionStage -> use .await()  (library bridge)
 future    Rx Single/Observable                      -> use rx3 await/asFlow

Why not just return a Deferred or CompletableDeferred? You can, but then cancellation of the caller does not reach the SDK, and you invent your own lifecycle. The two builders give you structured cancellation for free: the suspend version is tied to the caller's Job, the Flow version is tied to the collector.

Three things every bridge must answer: (1) who resumes, exactly once on every path; (2) what happens on cancellation (stop the work, unregister the listener); (3) which thread the callback runs on and whether the code you run there is safe. The resumption thread does not matter for correctness of resume: the continuation's dispatcher decides where the coroutine continues.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Callback<T> { fun onSuccess(value: T); fun onError(e: Throwable) }
interface Handle { fun cancel() }
class Sdk { fun fetch(id: String, cb: Callback<User>): Handle = TODO() }

suspend fun Sdk.fetchUser(id: String): User =
    suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
        val handle = fetch(id, object : Callback<User> {
            override fun onSuccess(value: User) = cont.resume(value)
            override fun onError(e: Throwable) = cont.resumeWithException(e)
        })
        cont.invokeOnCancellation { handle.cancel() }
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a Flow for a one-shot result (callers then need first() and you hide the contract).
  • Forgetting the error path, so the coroutine hangs forever when onError fires.
  • Forgetting cancellation: the SDK keeps working for a screen nobody is looking at.
  • Wrapping in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) "to make it async". The call is already async; IO only adds a thread hop.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the callback never fires? → The coroutine hangs until its parent is cancelled; add withTimeout at the call site or an SDK-level timeout.
  2. What if the callback fires synchronously inside fetch? → Fine: suspendCancellableCoroutine handles resume-before-block-returns; the call just returns without suspending.
  3. How do you expose a one-shot callback that can also be re-triggered (retry)? → Still a suspend function; retry is the caller's loop, each attempt is a fresh bridge call.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A 3-YOE answer writes the bridge and gets the happy path right. The senior asks first about cardinality and delivery thread, covers all three exit paths (success, error, cancel), and reaches for an existing await()/asFlow() before writing a custom one.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams routinely ship hand-rolled bridges with no cancellation hook; the symptom is network or sensor work continuing after the screen is gone, visible as battery and data drain rather than as a crash.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between suspendCoroutine and suspendCancellableCoroutine, and which one should you use by default?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic discriminator. Many candidates know both names but not what actually happens to a cancelled coroutine blocked in suspendCoroutine.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "suspendCoroutine gives you a plain Continuation that knows nothing about the coroutine's Job. If the coroutine is cancelled while suspended, nothing happens until the callback eventually resumes it, so a callback that never comes means a coroutine that never ends and a parent scope that cannot finish. suspendCancellableCoroutine gives a CancellableContinuation: cancellation resumes the suspension immediately with CancellationException and lets me run cleanup via invokeOnCancellation. Default to suspendCancellableCoroutine, always, for anything that touches I/O or can take time."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Both are the same primitive (suspendCoroutineUninterceptedOrReturn) with different wrappers.

  • suspendCoroutine { cont -> ... } wraps the continuation in a SafeContinuation. It guards against resume-before-suspend races, and a second resume throws IllegalStateException("Already resumed"). It does not link to the Job.
  • suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> ... } creates a CancellableContinuationImpl, which registers itself as a child-like handle on the coroutine's Job. When the Job is cancelled, the continuation is completed with the cancellation cause and the suspended caller is resumed with CancellationException, independently of the callback.
cancel() while suspended

suspendCoroutine                       suspendCancellableCoroutine
  Job cancelled                           Job cancelled
  continuation unaware                    continuation cancelled -> handlers run
  coroutine still parked                  coroutine resumes with CancellationException
  waits for callback (maybe forever)      callback later calls resume -> silently ignored
  parent scope.join() blocks              parent can complete

Important subtlety: suspendCoroutine is not "uncancellable" in a magical sense. When the callback eventually resumes it, the coroutine continues and sees the cancellation at its next cancellable suspension point. But in between, coroutineScope, withContext and join all wait for it. A screen scope that is cancelled but whose child is parked in suspendCoroutine stays alive, keeping the Activity, Fragment or ViewModel references captured in the lambdas alive.

When is plain suspendCoroutine acceptable? Only for operations that are genuinely instantaneous and not cancellable (for example adapting a synchronous-callback API that always calls back inline). In practice the cost of the cancellable version is tiny, so the rule is simply "always cancellable".

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: cancelling the caller does not cancel the call or release the coroutine
suspend fun Call.awaitBad(): Response = suspendCoroutine { cont ->
    enqueue(object : okhttp3.Callback {
        override fun onResponse(call: Call, response: Response) = cont.resume(response)
        override fun onFailure(call: Call, e: IOException) = cont.resumeWithException(e)
    })
}

// Correct
suspend fun Call.await(): Response = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }
    enqueue(object : okhttp3.Callback {
        override fun onResponse(call: Call, response: Response) = cont.resume(response)
        override fun onFailure(call: Call, e: IOException) = cont.resumeWithException(e)
    })
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking suspendCoroutine "swallows" cancellation. It does not throw; it just does not react, which is worse.
  • Using suspendCoroutine because autocomplete suggested it first.
  • Assuming withTimeout will rescue you. Timeout cancels the Job, and a non-cancellable suspension does not react, so the timeout fires late or only after the callback arrives.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens if the callback resumes a cancelled CancellableContinuation? → The resume is ignored, no exception. That is by design so late callbacks are harmless.
  2. Is there ever a reason for suspendCoroutine? → Almost never; maybe a trivially synchronous adapter in a library that must not depend on Job semantics.
  3. Where is the Job link established? → CancellableContinuationImpl.initCancellability() attaches a handle to the parent Job from the continuation's context before the block runs, so a Job already cancelled makes the block observe isCancelled immediately.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "one supports cancellation." Senior adds the consequence (a cancelled scope cannot finish while parked in the non-cancellable version, withTimeout becomes ineffective) and the late-callback rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-rolled suspendCoroutine wrapper around a slow SDK call made viewModelScope children outlive the ViewModel by 30 seconds, retaining the Activity via captured lambdas and showing up in LeakCanary as a "retained by Continuation".

questions.promptHtml: What does invokeOnCancellation do, when exactly does it run, and what rules must the handler follow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the cleanup hook of every bridge. Wrong assumptions (it runs on success, it runs on the coroutine's thread, it can suspend) cause real bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "It registers a handler on the CancellableContinuation that runs only if the continuation is cancelled, not when it is resumed normally. I use it to cancel the underlying request or unregister the listener. The handler can run on any thread, possibly concurrently with my callback, so it must be fast, non-blocking, thread-safe and must not throw. It is not a suspend context, and only one handler can be installed per continuation."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Contract (from the CancellableContinuation docs):

  • Runs when the continuation is cancelled (via Job cancellation or cont.cancel()); never on a normal resume or resumeWithException.
  • If the continuation is already cancelled when you install it, the handler runs immediately, so install it early without worrying about a gap.
  • At most one handler: a second invokeOnCancellation call throws IllegalStateException. If you have two things to clean up, combine them in one lambda.
  • Executes on whatever thread performed the cancellation, which is not necessarily the dispatcher of the coroutine. Therefore no touching UI, no blocking, no locks held across calls into the SDK that might call you back.
  • Exceptions thrown from it are wrapped in CompletionHandlerException and reported to the coroutine's exception handler / thread's uncaught handler. Treat as crash-capable.

Concurrency consequence: cancellation and the SDK callback can race.

thread A (callback)         thread B (cancel)
 cont.resume(value)          handler: handle.cancel()
   either order is possible; both are safe because:
   - resume on cancelled cont is ignored
   - cancelling an already finished request is a no-op (verify for your SDK)

If you need the cleanup to also run on success or error (for example always unregister a listener), use try/finally around the whole thing or unregister inside the callback too. invokeOnCancellation is not a finally.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun awaitCurrentLocation(
    lm: LocationManager, provider: String, executor: Executor
): Location? = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    val signal = CancellationSignal()
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { signal.cancel() }   // fast, non-blocking, thread-safe
    LocationManagerCompat.getCurrentLocation(lm, provider, signal, executor) { loc ->
        cont.resume(loc)                            // loc may be null; ignored if already cancelled
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing blocking work (closing a socket synchronously, runBlocking) in the handler.
  • Assuming it runs when the call finishes normally, so listeners registered for a successful path never unregister.
  • Installing it after a long synchronous registration; do it as soon as you have the handle.
  • Installing two handlers (for example by a helper wrapper plus your code).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you call a suspend function inside it? → No, it is a plain lambda; launch into an external scope if you must, but prefer a non-blocking cancel API.
  2. How is it different from try/finally around suspendCancellableCoroutine? → finally runs on all exits after the suspension returns, on the coroutine's thread; the handler runs at cancellation time, immediately, even if the coroutine has not resumed yet.
  3. What if the SDK cannot be cancelled? → Then cancellation still frees the coroutine, but the work continues; document it and make sure the result is discarded safely, using resume(value, onCancellation) if the result owns a resource.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "cleanup on cancel." Senior states the threading and single-handler contract, the race with the callback, and that it is not a finally.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A handler that called socket.close() synchronously on the main thread (cancellation came from viewModelScope.cancel() in onCleared) produced a StrictMode violation and a rare ANR.

questions.promptHtml: What happens if you call resume twice on a continuation? What about resuming after the coroutine was cancelled, or after resume but before the dispatcher runs the coroutine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real SDKs call callbacks twice, call both success and error, or fire after cancel. Interviewers want your mental model of the continuation state machine.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A second resume on a live continuation throws IllegalStateException: Already resumed. A resume on an already cancelled CancellableContinuation is silently ignored. And since 1.4, if I resume and the Job is cancelled before the dispatcher actually runs the coroutine, the suspension point throws CancellationException and the value I passed is dropped, which is the prompt cancellation guarantee. If that value is a resource like a Cursor or Response, I use resume(value) { cause, value, ctx -> value.close() } to release it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A CancellableContinuationImpl is a small atomic state machine:

 ACTIVE ──resume(v)──────────► RESUMED(v) ──dispatch──► coroutine continues with v
   │                              │
   │                              └─ second resume ► IllegalStateException("Already resumed...")
   └──cancel(cause)──► CANCELLED ──resume(v)──► ignored (no exception)
                          ▲
 RESUMED(v) and Job cancelled before dispatch runs the coroutine
   ──► (prompt cancellation) coroutine sees CancellationException, v dropped,
       onCancellation(cause, v, ctx) invoked if supplied

Key points:

  • Double resume on a cancelled continuation is tolerated; double resume on a completed one crashes. The crash is thrown on the callback thread, i.e. inside the SDK's own thread, so the stack trace points into the SDK and it can kill the process if the SDK has no handler.
  • resume, resumeWithException, and resumeWith(Result) all take the same one-shot slot. Success followed by error is a double resume.
  • The prompt cancellation guarantee exists because between resume and the actual continuation of the coroutine there is a dispatch (to Main, for instance). Without the guarantee a cancelled Activity's coroutine would still run its next line. With it, the coroutine does not observe the value after cancellation, so if the value must be disposed of, the bridge must do it: onCancellation is called if and only if the value was not delivered.
  • The 3-parameter onCancellation form (cause, value, context) is what the current API reference shows; older versions had a one-parameter experimental form. Check your version before relying on it.
  • isActive on the continuation is not a safe guard (check-then-act race). Use an atomic flag if the SDK may double-fire.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun Sdk.openCursor(q: String): Cursor =
    suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
        val done = AtomicBoolean(false)                  // SDK may fire twice
        query(q, object : Callback<Cursor> {
            override fun onSuccess(value: Cursor) {
                if (done.compareAndSet(false, true)) {
                    cont.resume(value) { _, c, _ -> c.close() }   // cancelled before delivery
                } else value.close()
            }
            override fun onError(e: Throwable) {
                if (done.compareAndSet(false, true)) cont.resumeWithException(e)
            }
        })
    }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping resume in try/catch (IllegalStateException) as a "fix". It hides a real SDK contract violation and still loses ordering guarantees.
  • Believing a late resume after cancel crashes (it does not) and then adding unnecessary guards, or the reverse.
  • Leaking the resumed value on prompt cancellation.
  • Never resuming on one path (for example onCancelled callback ignored), causing a hang.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where is the exception thrown, and who sees it? → On the thread that called the second resume, in the SDK's callback frame, not in your coroutine.
  2. Is suspendCoroutine the same here? → It also throws "Already resumed", but has no cancelled state to absorb late calls.
  3. How does tryResume relate? → It is @InternalCoroutinesApi, returns a token or null; avoid in app code and use an atomic flag.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it throws." Senior describes the three states, the ignore-on-cancelled rule, prompt cancellation and value disposal, and guards against SDK double-firing with an atomic.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An auth SDK invoked both onError and onSuccess after a retry inside the SDK; a coroutine bridge crashed 0.3% of sessions with "Already resumed" until an atomic guard went in.

questions.promptHtml: When do you use callbackFlow, channelFlow, and plain flow {}? Why can't I call emit from a callback inside flow {}?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of the context-preservation and sequential-emission rules and why channel-based builders exist.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "flow {} is sequential and context-preserving: emit must be called from the collector's coroutine, so I can't call it from a callback thread; it would throw or violate the flow invariant. channelFlow backs the flow with a channel, giving me a ProducerScope, so multiple child coroutines can send concurrently. callbackFlow is channelFlow specialised for callbacks: same machinery, but it enforces that the block ends with awaitClose so the listener is unregistered. Callbacks use callbackFlow, concurrent producers use channelFlow, everything sequential uses flow {}."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
flow {} creates a SafeFlow; emit is a suspend call that runs the downstream collect lambda directly on the producer's stack, in the collector's context. SafeCollector checks that the emitting context is the same as the collector's and that emissions are not concurrent. A callback runs on a foreign thread and is not a suspend function, so you cannot even call emit there without runBlocking (which blocks the SDK thread and trips the context check).

channelFlow {} and callbackFlow {} produce a ChannelFlowBuilder / CallbackFlowBuilder. On collection, the block runs inside a producer coroutine writing to a Channel (default capacity BUFFERED, 64, with SUSPEND overflow), and the collector reads from the channel. Because the channel is thread-safe, send/trySend can be called from any thread or coroutine.

flow {} channelFlow {} callbackFlow {}
Emit API emit (suspend, collector context only) send/trySend send/trySend
Concurrent producers No Yes Yes
Foreign-thread callbacks No Technically yes Yes (intended)
Must end with awaitClose n/a No Yes, enforced
Buffered No Yes (default 64) Yes (default 64)

callbackFlow is literally channelFlow plus a post-check: if the block returns while the channel is not closed it throws IllegalStateException ("'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block..."). That check exists because a channelFlow block that returns normally closes the channel (flow completes), which for a callback bridge would silently leave the listener registered and dead.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// callbacks
fun Sensor.readings(sm: SensorManager): Flow<Float> = callbackFlow {
    val l = object : SensorEventListener {
        override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) { trySend(e.values[0]) }
        override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, a: Int) = Unit
    }
    sm.registerListener(l, this@readings, SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_UI)
    awaitClose { sm.unregisterListener(l) }
}

// concurrent producers, no callback
fun merged(a: Api, b: Api): Flow<Item> = channelFlow {
    launch { a.items().collect { send(it) } }
    launch { b.items().collect { send(it) } }
}   // block returns after children complete; flow completes

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using flow {} plus withContext to emit: throws IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated. (The invariant itself is in the flow-fundamentals chunk.)
  • Using channelFlow for a listener and forgetting unregister, with no compiler or runtime warning.
  • Calling send (suspend) inside a non-suspend callback; use trySend.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not MutableSharedFlow for the callback? → That is a hot, always-on stream whose lifetime you manage; callbackFlow ties registration to collection, per-collector.
  2. Can I use callbackFlow for one-shot callbacks? → Yes but suspendCancellableCoroutine is simpler and honest about cardinality.
  3. What does callbackFlow do for conflate()? → .conflate() or .buffer(CONFLATED) right after fuses with the builder's own channel; it changes the channel's capacity rather than adding a second one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "callbackFlow for callbacks." Senior explains the SafeCollector reasons, the channel behind it, the enforced awaitClose, and capacity/fusion.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team emitted from a Firebase listener inside flow {} via runBlocking, deadlocking when the listener fired on the main thread while the collector ran there too.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly does awaitClose do inside callbackFlow, what happens if you omit it, and what does the lambda you pass to it do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: awaitClose is the single most common callbackFlow bug source (crash or leak). Interviewers want the mechanism, not "it keeps the flow open".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "awaitClose suspends the producer coroutine until the channel is closed or cancelled, which happens when the collector goes away or I/the callback call close(). Its lambda runs afterwards as cleanup: that's where I unregister the listener. Without it the block returns immediately, callbackFlow sees an open channel and throws IllegalStateException, so I find out in testing. The worse variant is a workaround like awaitCancellation() or an empty awaitClose {}: no crash, but the listener is never unregistered and keeps firing, leaking the callback and everything it captures."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
awaitClose(block) is suspendCancellableCoroutine on invokeOnClose, with try { ... } finally { block() }:

collector starts   -> producer coroutine runs your block
                      register listener
                      awaitClose suspends  <-- producer parked here
events:             -> callback thread: trySend(x) -> channel -> collector
collector cancels   -> channel cancelled -> awaitClose resumes -> finally { block() }
  (take(1), scope cancelled, first(), onCompletion with error downstream)
callback error      -> close(e) -> awaitClose resumes -> block() -> flow completes with e

Properties:

  • The cleanup lambda runs on every exit path (cancel, close(), close(cause)), in the producer coroutine, after cancellation. Because the coroutine is already cancelled, a suspend call inside the lambda would throw CancellationException immediately; keep cleanup non-suspending, or wrap it in withContext(NonCancellable).
  • It can run concurrently with the callback still firing on another thread: unregister must be thread-safe, and after unregister returns a late callback may still arrive. trySend into a closed channel just returns a failed ChannelResult, it does not throw.
  • Registering the listener can itself throw (permission, state). Do it inside the block so the exception propagates through the flow; if you registered successfully and something later fails, awaitClose is not reached, so wrap with try/catch or try { ... awaitClose() } finally.
  • Collector take(1) / first() cancels the producer after the first element, so cleanup is exercised constantly in real code.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun Firestore.docUpdates(path: String): Flow<DocumentSnapshot> = callbackFlow {
    val reg = collection(path).addSnapshotListener { snap, err ->
        when {
            err != null -> close(err)               // terminates flow with exception
            snap != null -> trySend(snap)
        }
    }
    awaitClose { reg.remove() }                     // always last; runs on cancel/close
}
// Looks like a fix, but leaks: listener never removed
callbackFlow { register(l); awaitCancellation() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting code after awaitClose {}; it only runs after close and usually not what you want.
  • Passing the wrong listener instance to unregister (a new lambda instance, not the registered one), so removal silently fails.
  • Not testing the cancel path (first()), so leaks go unnoticed.
  • Doing network work in the cleanup lambda.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the library throw instead of auto-cleaning? → It cannot know how to unregister your listener; the throw is a guardrail against a leak that would otherwise be silent.
  2. What if register is async and returns a Task? → Await it or attach failure listeners to close(e); unregister via the returned handle in the lambda.
  3. Is awaitClose the same as awaitCancellation? → No: it also resumes on close() (producer-side completion) and carries the cleanup lambda.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "needed so the flow doesn't finish; unregister inside." Senior knows the exact exception, the lambda timing and threading, the NonCancellable caveat, and the late-callback possibility.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An empty awaitClose {} copied from a snippet left a connectivity listener registered across 40 screen visits; after 40 visits each network change triggered 40 handlers.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate adds a battery-level stream to a diagnostics screen and says "works on my device". QA reports the app crashes on every open of the diagnostics screen, in debug and release (R8) builds alike, and Crashlytics shows IllegalStateException on 100% of opens of this screen (1.8% of sessions, 600k DAU). The code:

class BatteryRepo(private val ctx: Context) {
    fun levels(): Flow<Int> = callbackFlow {
        val receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
            override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) {
                val level = i.getIntExtra(BatteryManager.EXTRA_LEVEL, -1)
                trySend(level)
            }
        }
        ctx.registerReceiver(receiver, IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED))
    }
}

// ViewModel
val level = repo.levels().stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, 0)

Stack: java.lang.IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block. at kotlinx.coroutines.flow.CallbackFlowBuilder.collectTo.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why it surfaces at runtime and not compile time, and fix it. Then tell me what the tempting wrong fixes are.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in try/catch" or "add awaitClose() with nothing in it". The first hides the crash and the flow is dead; the second keeps the flow open but still leaks the receiver forever. Also blames R8 (red herring) or the stateIn (red herring).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it deterministic (yes, 100% of opens: points to a structural bug not a race)? Which Context is passed (Activity vs application: a registered receiver on an Activity leaks it)? Is the stream supposed to live only while the screen is shown? Does the minimum API need RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED flags on Android 14 (sticky system broadcast, not applicable, but check)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix via remote config to hide the diagnostics tile, or ship a one-line fix: it's small enough to fix directly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) block returns without awaitClose, callbackFlow throws (matches stack exactly); (b) stateIn(Eagerly) starts collecting immediately so the crash happens at ViewModel creation (explains "on open"); (c) R8 stripping (stack contradicts); (d) receiver registered on wrong context (separate latent leak).
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the stack: the message is exact. Reproduce with a unit test: repo.levels().first() throws on current code. Confirm receiver leakage separately with LeakCanary/dumpsys activity broadcasts.
  5. Root cause: The builder lambda finishes after registerReceiver. A channelFlow block that returns closes the channel and completes the flow; callbackFlow instead verifies the channel was closed by someone else (callback close() or cancellation) and throws if not. Compile time cannot know a runtime channel state, hence a runtime check. Eagerly just means it blows up when the ViewModel is created.
  6. Fix:
fun levels(): Flow<Int> = callbackFlow {
    val receiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
        override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) { trySend(i.getIntExtra(BatteryManager.EXTRA_LEVEL, -1)) }
    }
    // Sticky broadcast: registerReceiver returns the current value immediately
    ctx.registerReceiver(receiver, IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED))
        ?.let { trySend(it.getIntExtra(BatteryManager.EXTRA_LEVEL, -1)) }
    awaitClose { ctx.unregisterReceiver(receiver) }
}.distinctUntilChanged()

Use the application context. Short term: the above. Long term: switch the upstream sharing to WhileSubscribed(5_000) (covered in the sharing chunk) so the receiver is unregistered when the screen is gone. 7. Prevention: Unit test per bridge that collects first() and asserts unregister was called (fake context). A shared lint/detekt check or code review checklist: every callbackFlow ends with awaitClose containing a matching unregister. Wrap the pattern in a small helper once. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not catching IllegalStateException. Not awaitCancellation() (compiles, no cleanup). Not close() at the end (flow completes immediately and emits nothing useful). Not runBlocking anything.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if unregisterReceiver throws IllegalArgumentException: Receiver not registered? → Happens if registration failed or cleanup runs twice; guard with a registered flag and register inside try.
  • What if the broadcast arrives after cancellation? → trySend on a closed channel returns a failed result; no throw. Safe.
  • What if two screens collect? → Each collection registers its own receiver; if you want one registration, share the flow upstream.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a diagnostics module: the snippet came from a blog and was copied across five repositories; only the one with Eagerly crashed visibly. The four others used Lazily and the crash hid behind a rarely opened screen for two releases.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests try/catch or empty awaitClose; cannot explain why it throws.
  • Hire: Adds awaitClose { unregister }, explains channel-closed check, mentions application context.
  • Strong hire: Also covers sticky initial value, sharing policy for lifecycle, a test that exercises the cancel path, and rejects the silent-leak workarounds with reasons.

questions.promptHtml: How do you consume a Google Play services / Firebase Task<T> from a coroutine? What does await() do on success, failure and cancellation, and what does it not do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tasks are everywhere in Android SDKs (Firebase Auth, FCM token, Fused Location, in-app review). Interviewers check you do not hand-write listeners and that you know the cancellation limit.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I add kotlinx-coroutines-play-services and call task.await(). It suspends, returns the result on success, throws the task's exception on failure, and throws CancellationException if the Task itself was cancelled. If the calling coroutine is cancelled, await() stops waiting and throws, but a plain Task has no cancel API, so the underlying work keeps running unless I passed the SDK a CancellationToken. For SDK calls that accept a CancellationTokenSource, I use the overload that wires coroutine cancellation to it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Task<T> is Play services' promise type with addOnSuccessListener, addOnFailureListener, addOnCanceledListener. The await() extension in kotlinx-coroutines-play-services is a suspendCancellableCoroutine bridge:

  1. If the task is already complete, it returns immediately without suspending (success value, or throws the exception; if cancelled, throws CancellationException).
  2. Otherwise it attaches a completion listener (on a direct executor, so the continuation is resumed on whatever thread the Task completes, and the coroutine's dispatcher then redispatches it).
  3. On coroutine cancellation it only abandons the wait. Since Task offers no cancel(), the work continues. The library has a await(cancellationTokenSource) overload in recent versions which calls cancel() on the source when the coroutine is cancelled; check your artifact version, and the SDK method must itself accept a CancellationToken (for example FusedLocationProviderClient.getCurrentLocation(priority, token)).

Other utilities in the artifact: Deferred<T>.asTask() (coroutine to Task, for exposing to Java callers) and Task<T>.asDeferred().

Exceptions from await() on failure are the original Exception (for example FirebaseAuthInvalidCredentialsException, ApiException), so you can catch typed ones. Remember that catching Exception also catches CancellationException; rethrow it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle: implementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-play-services:<same as coroutines>")
suspend fun FirebaseAuth.signInSafely(email: String, pass: String): Result<FirebaseUser> =
    try {
        Result.success(signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, pass).await().user!!)
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        throw e                                  // never swallow
    } catch (e: FirebaseAuthException) {
        Result.failure(e)
    }

// Cancellable location fetch
suspend fun FusedLocationProviderClient.currentOrNull(): Location? {
    val cts = CancellationTokenSource()
    return try {
        getCurrentLocation(Priority.PRIORITY_BALANCED_POWER_ACCURACY, cts.token).await()
    } finally {
        cts.cancel()                              // no-op if already completed; stops work on cancellation
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hand-writing addOnSuccessListener / addOnFailureListener and forgetting addOnCanceledListener, so a cancelled Task hangs the coroutine.
  • Assuming coroutine cancellation cancels the Firebase operation.
  • Catching Exception around await() and swallowing CancellationException.
  • Mixing artifact versions: use the same version as kotlinx-coroutines-core.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the Task completes on the main thread but you want work off it? → await() resumes on the coroutine's own dispatcher; the Task's thread is irrelevant for your code.
  2. How is Tasks.await (blocking) different? → It blocks the calling thread and must not run on the main thread; kotlinx await() suspends.
  3. How do you expose a suspend function to Java code that expects a Task? → scope.async { ... }.asTask().

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use .await()." Senior adds the failure/cancel semantics, that coroutine cancellation does not cancel the Task, the CancellationTokenSource pattern, and the swallowed-CancellationException trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "fetch location for check-in" screen kept the GPS engine running for 30 seconds after users left because the Task could not be cancelled; fixed by passing a CancellationToken through await.

questions.promptHtml: How do you bridge ListenableFuture (CameraX, Media3, WorkManager) and CompletableFuture into coroutines? What happens to the future when the coroutine is cancelled, and in the other direction?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Jetpack still exposes Guava ListenableFuture widely. The question tests whether you know the library await() extensions and the two-way cancellation propagation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "For ListenableFuture I use await() from kotlinx-coroutines-guava or from androidx.concurrent:concurrent-futures-ktx. For CompletableFuture/CompletionStage I use kotlinx.coroutines.future.await. Both are cancellable and one-shot. If my coroutine is cancelled, the future is cancelled too, so the producer can stop; if the future is cancelled, await() throws CancellationException. Futures are one-shot, so no Flow here. I never call future.get() on the main thread because that blocks."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A ListenableFuture<V> adds addListener(Runnable, Executor) to Future<V>. await() is a bridge using that: it adds a listener, and on completion reads the result with getDone-style semantics (no blocking since it is complete), mapping:

  • completed value -> return;
  • ExecutionException -> throws its cause;
  • cancelled future -> CancellationException.

Cancellation propagates both ways, which is the main point:

  • Coroutine cancel while suspended -> future.cancel(false) (Guava version; the CompletableFuture doc says the CompletableFuture corresponding to the stage is cancelled). mayInterruptIfRunning semantics differ by implementation; do not rely on thread interruption.
  • Future cancel -> await() throws CancellationException. Note that this makes the awaiting coroutine look cancelled and, depending on the structure, can silently cancel a parent branch. If a future can be cancelled by someone else, translate that case (catch (e: CancellationException) { if (coroutineContext.isActive) handleFutureCancelled() else throw e }).

Reverse bridges: future { ... } (Guava and kotlinx.coroutines.future) starts a coroutine and returns a future; cancelling the future cancels the coroutine. Deferred.asCompletableFuture() and ListenableFuture.asDeferred() also exist.

Version notes: CompletionStage.await lived in kotlinx-coroutines-jdk8 historically; in recent releases (1.7+, verify for your version) it is part of core on JVM. On Android, CompletableFuture needs API 24+ (or desugaring); ListenableFuture has no such constraint.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// CameraX
suspend fun Context.cameraProvider(): ProcessCameraProvider =
    ProcessCameraProvider.getInstance(this).await()       // androidx.concurrent:concurrent-futures-ktx

// WorkManager: ListenableFuture<List<WorkInfo>>
suspend fun WorkManager.statusOf(name: String): List<WorkInfo> =
    getWorkInfosForUniqueWork(name).await()

// coroutine -> Java API wanting a ListenableFuture
fun CoroutineScope.loadFuture(): ListenableFuture<User> =
    future { repo.load() }                                 // kotlinx-coroutines-guava

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling .get() in a suspend function on Main or Default. It blocks the thread (and a suspend function does not make blocking calls safe).
  • Using Futures.addCallback plus a manual continuation.
  • Assuming cancelling the coroutine stops a computation running inside the future; only cooperative futures stop.
  • Forgetting that CompletableFuture.await on Android below API 24 needs desugaring.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does await() change which thread your code resumes on? → The future's listener runs on the future's executor (often direct), then dispatch goes back to the coroutine's dispatcher.
  2. Can a ListenableFuture be consumed multiple times? → Yes, await() can be called repeatedly; each reads the completed result.
  3. Why is future.get() inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO) still worse than await()? → It pins one IO thread per pending future and cannot be cancelled cooperatively.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "await()". Senior states two-way cancellation, the get() blocking hazard, the future-cancelled-looks-like-coroutine-cancelled trap, and the reverse future {} bridge for Java interop.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Camera binding on a screen with fast tab switching leaked providers because futures were .get()-ed on a worker; swapping to await() allowed cancellation to propagate and removed ANRs from get() on main.

questions.contextHtml:
A ride-sharing app (1.5M DAU, mix of Android 8-14, many low-end devices) streams driver location. A teammate's wrapper:

fun FusedLocationProviderClient.updates(req: LocationRequest): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
    val cb = object : LocationCallback() {
        override fun onLocationResult(r: LocationResult) {
            r.lastLocation?.let { trySend(it) }
        }
    }
    requestLocationUpdates(req, cb, Looper.getMainLooper())
    awaitClose { removeLocationUpdates(cb) }
}

Crashlytics shows SecurityException crashes on 0.6% of sessions after Android 11 users revoke "precise" permission mid-session, p95 main-thread frame time rises 12% on the tracking screen, and the system status bar GPS indicator sometimes stays on a few seconds after leaving. Product also wants "offline GPS off" to surface as a UI message.
questions.promptHtml: Review this wrapper. What do you change and why, and what stays the same?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, awaitClose is there." Misses error propagation (the Task returned by requestLocationUpdates fails separately), thread choice, buffering and permission handling. Or rewrites it into a SharedFlow global singleton.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What update interval and priority (500 ms high accuracy vs 10 s balanced)? Is the screen foreground-only or is there a foreground service? Does every consumer need every fix, or latest only? Who owns permission checks? Do we need availability changes (GPS off) or only fixes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Catch SecurityException at registration and turn it into a flow error, rather than a crash, in a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) requestLocationUpdates throws SecurityException synchronously inside the callbackFlow block; thrown into the collector; with no catch, it crashes the ViewModel scope. (b) The Task returned by the call fails asynchronously (e.g. settings resolution failure) and the code ignores it, so flow looks alive but is dead. (c) The callback is on the main looper so every fix does work on Main (trySend itself is cheap, but downstream mapping is not if flowOn is missing; jank source). (d) trySend into default buffer 64 and a slow collector: drops are possible when buffer full; for location, latest is what matters. (e) GPS indicator lag is removeLocationUpdates being async (Task), not a bug; red herring unless it never completes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Crashlytics stack for SecurityException origin; reproduce by revoking permission via adb shell pm revoke; Perfetto/system trace for main-thread slices from onLocationResult; unit test with a fake client; dumpsys location to see lingering registrations.
  5. Root cause: The wrapper treats registration as infallible and one-dimensional: permission failures (sync), async failures (Task), and backpressure semantics are all unmodelled, and callbacks are delivered on Main by choice.
  6. Fix:
@SuppressLint("MissingPermission")
fun FusedLocationProviderClient.updates(
    req: LocationRequest,
    looper: Looper,                                  // inject a HandlerThread looper
): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
    val cb = object : LocationCallback() {
        override fun onLocationResult(r: LocationResult) { r.lastLocation?.let { trySend(it) } }
        override fun onLocationAvailability(a: LocationAvailability) { /* optionally surface */ }
    }
    try {
        requestLocationUpdates(req, cb, looper)
            .addOnFailureListener { close(it) }       // async failure -> flow error
    } catch (e: SecurityException) {
        close(e); return@callbackFlow                  // still must not skip cleanup: nothing registered
    }
    awaitClose { removeLocationUpdates(cb) }
}.conflate()                                          // latest fix wins for a map pin

Short term: ship the try/catch + failure listener. Long term: injected looper, permission gate before collecting (the screen only collects when granted), catch {} mapping to UI state. Sharing one upstream between screens is the job of shareIn/stateIn covered in the sharing chunk. 7. Prevention: A fake FusedLocationProviderClient test asserting removeLocationUpdates on cancel and close(e) on failure; QA matrix for permission revoke mid-session; a custom lint/review rule "no requestLocationUpdates outside the wrapper". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not UNLIMITED buffer (memory growth if UI is stalled). Not trySendBlocking on the location thread. Not a global hot SharedFlow that never stops GPS. conflate() is wrong if every fix is a billable trip-distance sample; then use buffer(UNLIMITED) upstream of a persisting consumer, or write to disk in the callback.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the fix delivery is every 100 ms? → Interval is a battery decision at the request; the Flow only adapts; use conflate plus sample only if the UI cannot keep up.
  • What if you need the last known location first? → Emit lastLocation.await() inside the flow before awaiting close, accepting it may be stale and null.
  • What if two screens need updates? → One shared upstream, otherwise two registrations double the work.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a delivery app: the map-follow feature worked in QA but killed batteries in the field, because unregistration relied on a collector that lived in a singleton scope. The wrapper was fine; the missing piece was a sharing policy with a stop timeout.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Approves as is, or blames trySend.
  • Hire: Catches sync and async errors, moves callbacks off Main, picks conflate with reason.
  • Strong hire: Also separates availability vs fix, explains why awaitClose cleanup is Task-async, tests with fakes, and keeps sharing policy out of the wrapper.

questions.promptHtml: Firebase Realtime/Firestore listeners and SensorManager both use "register, receive many, unregister". How do you wrap them as Flows? What differs between them, and what do you watch out for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks you can apply the callbackFlow recipe to two real APIs with different error and rate characteristics, not just recite it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Both use callbackFlow with awaitClose doing the unregister. Firestore's addSnapshotListener returns a ListenerRegistration and delivers an error through the same callback, so I map errors to close(e) and values to trySend. Sensors deliver at high frequency with no error channel, so the main decisions are sampling rate, which thread (pass a Handler), and buffer policy, usually conflate(). If the Firebase SDK already ships a snapshots()/dataObjects() Kotlin extension, I use that instead of my own."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Shared recipe: register inside the block, hold the handle, awaitClose { unregister(handle) }. The differences:

Concern Firestore / RTDB listener SensorManager
Rate Event-driven, low Up to hundreds of Hz
Error Delivered to callback (FirebaseFirestoreException / DatabaseError); listener is dead after an error None; registration returns Boolean (false if sensor unavailable)
First value Initial snapshot on attach, possibly from cache (metadata.isFromCache) Next sensor event only
Unregister handle ListenerRegistration.remove() / removeEventListener(l) unregisterListener(l)
Thread Callback on main thread by default (Firestore) Handler you pass, else main
Buffer Default fine, or conflate() for state conflate(); firehose handling belongs to the backpressure section

Details that matter:

  • Firestore: after a listener error the SDK removes the listener; so close(e) is correct, and a retry means collecting the flow again (a retryWhen upstream of your UI state). Do not trySend the exception as data unless your domain wants it.
  • Realtime Database ValueEventListener has onCancelled(DatabaseError); map to close(error.toException()).
  • Sensors: registerListener returning false means no such sensor or no permission (for example BODY_SENSORS on health sensors); close the flow with an exception. Use SENSOR_DELAY_* constants or microseconds and note the Android 12+ cap of 200 Hz without the HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS permission.
  • SensorEvent.values arrays are reused by the system. Copying the data out (event.values.copyOf()) is mandatory when you buffer; sending the same array leads to every queued element showing the latest values. This is a classic silent bug.
  • Firebase's main-thread callbacks mean mapping heavy documents (toObject) happens on Main unless you flowOn downstream or pass an executor to addSnapshotListener(executor, listener).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun Query.snapshotsFlow(): Flow<QuerySnapshot> = callbackFlow {
    val reg = addSnapshotListener { snap, err ->
        if (err != null) close(err) else if (snap != null) trySend(snap)
    }
    awaitClose { reg.remove() }
}

fun SensorManager.accel(handler: Handler): Flow<FloatArray> = callbackFlow {
    val s = getDefaultSensor(Sensor.TYPE_ACCELEROMETER)
        ?: run { close(IllegalStateException("No accelerometer")); return@callbackFlow }
    val l = object : SensorEventListener {
        override fun onSensorChanged(e: SensorEvent) { trySend(e.values.copyOf()) }   // copy!
