        override fun onAccuracyChanged(s: Sensor?, accuracy: Int) = Unit
    }
    if (!registerListener(l, s, SensorManager.SENSOR_DELAY_GAME, handler)) {
        close(IllegalStateException("registerListener failed")); return@callbackFlow
    }
    awaitClose { unregisterListener(l) }
}.conflate()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sending e.values without copyOf().
  • Treating Firestore error as non-terminal.
  • Registering the same listener object for several sensors/flows and unregistering all of them from one cancel.
  • Heavy deserialisation on the callback (main) thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why close(e) and not cancel(...)? → close(e) completes the flow with exception e, observable by catch; cancel is cancellation semantics. See the error-mapping question below.
  2. How do you get the initial value for sensors? → There is none; seed with onStart or accept the first event.
  3. Firestore snapshot with isFromCache? → Deliver metadata with the value so UI can show stale state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: wrap both the same way. Senior distinguishes error channels, thread defaults, reused value arrays, and sampling limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Step-counter UI showed identical values for all buffered samples after introducing buffer(), root cause: SensorEvent.values aliasing.

questions.contextHtml:
An order-tracking screen in a delivery app shows events from a socket-like SDK. After the team added repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) collection, support reports "each status update plays the notification sound 2, 3, then 5 times" the longer a session goes on. The analytics team sees order_status_received events per user growing with the number of times the user backgrounded and returned (average 4.1 events per real update, 480k DAU).

class TrackingRepo(private val sdk: TrackingSdk) {          // app-scoped singleton
    private val bus = MutableSharedFlow<OrderEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 64)
    val events: Flow<OrderEvent> = bus.asSharedFlow()

    // keeps the SDK subscription alive while collected
    fun subscribe(orderId: String): Flow<Unit> = callbackFlow {
        val l = TrackingListener { e -> bus.tryEmit(e) }
        sdk.addListener(orderId, l)
        awaitClose { sdk.removeListener(orderId, TrackingListener { e -> bus.tryEmit(e) }) }
    }
}
// Fragment
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        launch { vm.subscribe(orderId).collect() }
        launch { vm.events.collect { sound.play(); render(it) } }
    }
}

Red herrings: the team suspects repeatOnLifecycle "collecting twice", and a recent SDK upgrade.
questions.promptHtml: Find why the number of deliveries grows with each background/foreground cycle, prove it, and fix it. Then say what else could cause duplicates even after the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Removes repeatOnLifecycle or adds distinctUntilChanged() to hide duplicates. Blames the SDK upgrade without evidence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does removeListener compare by identity or equals? Are duplicates equal events (same id)? Is the repository a singleton? Do we see growth after rotation too? Does the count reset on process restart (yes would imply in-memory registration)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side/clients-side dedupe by event id behind a flag to stop the sound spam; this is containment only, not the fix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Unregister uses a new listener instance, so removeListener removes nothing: every STOP/START leaves one more live listener. (b) repeatOnLifecycle is working correctly: it cancels on STOP and restarts on START, so each restart calls the callbackFlow block again; that is by design and harmless when cleanup works. (c) SDK upgrade changed removal semantics. (d) Two collectors in the screen.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log registration and removal with System.identityHashCode(l); a debug counter of live listeners; unit test with a fake SDK recording add/remove and asserting zero live listeners after first() or cancel; LeakCanary for the retained lambdas capturing the fragment's trySend chain.
  5. Root cause: awaitClose { removeListener(orderId, TrackingListener {...}) } constructs a different object than the one registered, so removal is a no-op. The SDK keeps invoking every stale listener, and each one forwards into the same app-scoped bus, so a single server event is emitted once per leaked listener. Delivery count equals 1 + number of STOP/START cycles, which matches the 4.1 average. Note the subtlety: had the listener sent into its own per-collection channel (closed on cancel), stale listeners would only waste CPU; the duplicates appear because the stale listeners write to shared state.
  6. Fix:
fun subscribe(orderId: String): Flow<Unit> = callbackFlow {
    val l = TrackingListener { e -> bus.tryEmit(e) }
    sdk.addListener(orderId, l)
    awaitClose { sdk.removeListener(orderId, l) }     // same instance
}

Short term: that one line plus the fake-SDK test. Long term: if several screens need the stream, one shared upstream (shareIn/stateIn with a stop timeout) so there is exactly one registration; make the SDK wrapper return a disposable handle so you cannot pass a different instance. 7. Prevention: Test "N collect/cancel cycles leave 0 listeners"; code-review rule: the registered object is a named val used in both places; add listener-count assertions to debug builds. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not distinctUntilChanged (masks leak, keeps CPU and memory growth). Not removing repeatOnLifecycle (then the stream runs in background). Not GlobalScope. Dedup by id is still reasonable as defence in depth if the SDK is at-least-once.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the SDK is at-least-once by design? → Dedupe by event id downstream and keep idempotent handlers.
  • What if two fragments collect the same cold flow? → Two registrations, two deliveries each, by design; share upstream if the SDK charges per listener.
  • What if the SDK only supports a single listener per order? → Registering again silently replaces the first; see the single-listener question on API constraints.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a chat badge counter grew by one on every tab switch. The leak was a lambda created twice ({...} is a new object each time), a classic when listeners are compared by identity. A unit test counting live listeners caught it in 10 minutes once someone thought to write it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Removes lifecycle collection or masks with distinct.
  • Hire: Spots the mismatched instance in removeListener, fixes it, explains why repeatOnLifecycle is not at fault.
  • Strong hire: Proves with a counting fake, proposes shared upstream and idempotent handling, and discusses at-least-once delivery.

questions.promptHtml: How does Retrofit make suspend fun getUser(): User work? What happens under the hood when it is called and when the calling coroutine is cancelled?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most common real-world callback bridge. Interviewers use it to see if you can connect the CPS transformation, suspendCancellableCoroutine, and OkHttp cancellation, and know the quirks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Since Retrofit 2.6.0 a suspend interface method compiles to a method with a trailing Continuation parameter and an Object return type. Retrofit detects that parameter, creates a Call<T> for the real response type, and calls an internal Call<T>.await() extension that uses suspendCancellableCoroutine with enqueue. onResponse resumes with the body or an HttpException, onFailure resumes with the throwable, and invokeOnCancellation { cancel() } cancels the OkHttp call. The request runs on OkHttp's dispatcher threads, which makes Retrofit suspend functions main-safe."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Compile-time shape: suspend fun getUser(): User becomes Object getUser(Continuation<? super User>) in bytecode (CPS). Retrofit's RequestFactory checks whether the last parameter type is Continuation; if so, it extracts the continuation's type argument as the response type and flags the method as isKotlinSuspendFunction.

HttpServiceMethod then builds a SuspendForBody or SuspendForResponse adapter (depending on whether the declared type is Response<T>):

call getUser(cont)
  -> SuspendForBody.adapt(call, args)
       continuation = last arg
       call = callAdapter.adapt(call)         (a plain Call<ResponseT>)
       KotlinExtensions.await(call, continuation)
             suspendCancellableCoroutine { c ->
                 c.invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel() }
                 call.enqueue(object: Callback<T> {
                     onResponse: 2xx & body -> c.resume(body)
                                 2xx & null body -> resumeWithException(KotlinNullPointerException(...))
                                 non-2xx -> c.resumeWithException(HttpException(response))
                     onFailure -> c.resumeWithException(t)
                 })
             }

Consequences:

  • Main-safe: enqueue runs on OkHttp's dispatcher; the coroutine resumes on its own dispatcher afterwards. You do not need withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
  • Cancellation: the coroutine's cancellation calls Call.cancel(), which aborts the OkHttp call; the interceptor chain sees IOException("Canceled"), but the continuation is already cancelled so it is ignored.
  • Errors: HTTP errors become retrofit2.HttpException (non-2xx), IO problems IOException, parsing errors from the converter (for example JsonDataException). Returning Response<T> gives you the raw response and no HttpException.
  • Checked exceptions: a Java dynamic proxy would wrap checked exceptions not declared on the method into UndeclaredThrowableException. Retrofit works around this with an internal suspendAndThrow trick that resumes the exception through a dispatcher so it surfaces as the original type.
  • Custom CallAdapters (for example Rx) are bypassed for suspend functions in the response-type sense: the adapter must support Call<T> itself (the default does).
  • Nullable bodies: declare suspend fun x(): User? or Unit for 204 responses to avoid the KotlinNullPointerException for empty bodies.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Api {
    @GET("users/{id}") suspend fun user(@Path("id") id: String): User            // body or throws
    @GET("users/{id}") suspend fun userResponse(@Path("id") id: String): Response<User>
    @DELETE("users/{id}") suspend fun delete(@Path("id") id: String)             // Unit
}

suspend fun load(id: String): Result<User> = try {
    Result.success(api.user(id))
} catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
  catch (e: HttpException) { Result.failure(e) }
  catch (e: IOException) { Result.failure(e) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) and thinking it is required.
  • runCatching { api.user() } swallowing CancellationException.
  • Interceptors using runBlocking: they run on OkHttp threads, which is a different problem (blocking) than main thread, but still creates thread starvation under load.
  • Ignoring 204/empty bodies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does cancelling the coroutine stop the server from processing? → No, it aborts the client socket; non-idempotent POSTs may still complete on the server. Use idempotency keys.
  2. How does Call.execute() differ? → Blocking, runs on the caller thread; never on Main.
  3. How would you retry only on IO errors? → Catch IOException in a retry loop; do not retry on HttpException 4xx; cancellation passes through.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Retrofit supports suspend, main-safe." Senior knows the detection mechanism, the await bridge with invokeOnCancellation, the exception mapping and the POST-cancellation semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams retried POST payments after cancellation because the user left the screen; the server had already charged. Cancellation is client-side only.

questions.promptHtml: You are incrementally moving from RxJava 3 to coroutines. What does kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 give you, and what behaviours (cancellation, backpressure, nulls, error handling) must you reason about at each boundary?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers inherit Rx code. This question probes the bridge semantics, not Rx-vs-Flow opinions (the operator mapping and migration strategy belong to a later chunk).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The artifact has two directions. Rx to coroutines: Single/Maybe/Completable.await(), Observable.awaitFirst/awaitLast/awaitSingle, and ObservableSource/Publisher.asFlow(). Coroutines to Rx: rxSingle {}, rxMaybe {}, rxCompletable {}, rxObservable {}, rxFlowable {}, Flow.asObservable()/asFlowable(). At every boundary I check: cancellation (disposing the Rx subscription when the coroutine is cancelled, and cancelling the coroutine when the Rx subscriber disposes), backpressure (hot Observables have none, so the bridge must buffer), nulls (Rx3 forbids null), and errors (Rx onError becomes thrown exceptions from await/Flow, undeliverable errors go to RxJavaPlugins)."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rx to coroutines:

  • Single<T>.await() subscribes with a SingleObserver and bridges via suspendCancellableCoroutine: on coroutine cancel it disposes the Disposable. Maybe.await() throws NoSuchElementException when empty; awaitSingleOrNull-style variants return null.
  • Observable.awaitFirst/awaitLast/awaitSingle take the first/last/only element and throw if empty or (for awaitSingle) more than one; awaitFirst disposes the upstream after the first item.
  • asFlow() turns the source into a cold Flow: subscription happens on collection, disposal on collector cancellation. For Publisher/Flowable the bridge requests items according to the collector's demand (backpressure-aware); for ObservableSource (no backpressure concept) items push in regardless, so the bridge has to buffer; add an explicit buffer(...)/conflate() to choose the policy instead of trusting the default (verify the default capacity for your version).

Coroutines to Rx:

  • rxSingle(context) { ... } etc. start a coroutine per subscription; disposing the Rx subscription cancels the coroutine.
  • Exceptions thrown from the block become onError; if the subscriber has already disposed, the exception is undeliverable and is routed to RxJavaPlugins.onError, which by default crashes on RxJava 3. Install a handler for UndeliverableException as you would in Rx-only code.
  • Flow.asObservable(context) / asFlowable() collect the flow on context (default EmptyCoroutineContext, so on the thread the subscriber triggers or the default scope's dispatcher; set it explicitly).
  • Null: Rx 3 forbids null values, Single<Foo?> is invalid; a coroutine block returning null into rxSingle leads to NPE. Use rxMaybe (null becomes empty) or wrap with Optional.
Rx world                              Coroutine world
Single/Maybe/Completable  --await-->  suspend fun
Observable/Flowable       --asFlow--> Flow (cold, cancel disposes)
rxSingle{} / rxObservable{} <------   suspend / ProducerScope code
Flow                      --asObservable/asFlowable--> Rx (dispose cancels collector)

Migration advice at the seam: convert at the repository boundary, keep one direction per layer, and convert down the stack first (data layer to Flow) while UI still wraps Flow with asObservable for legacy consumers, or the reverse, but never ping-pong inside one pipeline.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Rx -> coroutines
suspend fun loadProfile(api: RxApi): Profile = api.profile().await()          // Single<Profile>
fun ticks(rx: Observable<Long>): Flow<Long> = rx.asFlow().conflate()

// coroutines -> Rx
fun profileRx(repo: Repo): Single<Profile> = rxSingle(Dispatchers.IO) { repo.profile() }
fun eventsRx(f: Flow<Event>): Observable<Event> = f.asObservable(Dispatchers.Default)

// Global once: avoid process crashes from undeliverable errors
RxJavaPlugins.setErrorHandler { if (it !is UndeliverableException) throw it }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping every Rx stream in suspendCoroutine manually.
  • Missing RxJavaPlugins.setErrorHandler, so a cancelled rxSingle that throws crashes the app.
  • Using the rx2 artifact with RxJava 3 (they are separate: rx2, rx3).
  • Null results and Maybe emptiness surprises.
  • Ignoring schedulers: Rx observeOn(mainThread()) plus asFlow() still delivers on the collector's context; the Rx scheduler is the producer-side thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does disposal propagate? → Collector cancel disposes the Rx source; Rx dispose cancels the coroutine started by rx* builders.
  2. Which is better for an event bus: PublishSubject + asFlow() or SharedFlow? → Migrate to MutableSharedFlow; if a bridge is needed, document that asFlow() of a hot subject subscribes per collector and can miss events before collection.
  3. What about Rx Schedulers.io() work you want to cancel from a coroutine? → Disposal interrupts the thread only if Rx uses interrupt; blocking work may not stop. Use await() and ensure the source's work respects disposal.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "there are await and asFlow." Senior covers disposal in both directions, hot-source backpressure, null policy, the undeliverable exception handler, and a seam-by-seam migration plan.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: During an Rx-to-coroutines migration, a cancelled rxSingle that later threw crashed 0.2% of sessions with UndeliverableException until the global error handler was installed.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (900k DAU) wraps a third-party identity-verification SDK for the KYC flow. After release 7.12, Crashlytics shows a new top crash: 0.35% of sessions, 100% on the KYC screen, from the SDK's own callback thread:

Fatal Exception: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Already resumed
    at kotlin.coroutines.SafeContinuation.resumeWith(SafeContinuation.kt:...)
    at com.app.kyc.SdkBridgeKt$verify$2$1.onFailure(SdkBridge.kt:41)
    at com.vendor.idv.Session.dispatchResult(Session.java:...)
Thread: vendor-callback-3

The bridge:

suspend fun IdvSdk.verify(doc: Doc): Verdict = suspendCoroutine { cont ->
    start(doc, object : IdvCallback {
        override fun onSuccess(v: Verdict) = cont.resume(v)
        override fun onFailure(e: IdvError) = cont.resumeWithException(e.toException())
    })
}

Release notes of 7.12 list: SDK upgrade 4.1 to 4.3, a new 20-second timeout in the ViewModel (withTimeout(20_000)), and a retry button. Red herrings: the team suspects a coroutines upgrade and a threading bug in the ViewModel.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix this, and tell me what the contract changes should be so it cannot recur.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Wraps resume in try/catch, or replaces suspendCoroutine with suspendCancellableCoroutine and declares victory, not knowing why it fired twice. Blames the VM thread.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the crash start exactly with the SDK bump (staged rollout comparison)? Does the vendor document "onFailure after onSuccess" cases, for example a late network error after a cached verdict? Is it correlated with the timeout path or with the retry button? Do users who crash have a poor network (device/country distribution)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout; ship a hotfix with an atomic guard that ignores any second callback. Or remotely disable the new SDK path if flagged.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SDK 4.3 can invoke both onSuccess and onFailure (for example failure after a delivered verdict, from a background upload) = double resume. (b) The retry button starts a second start() on the same bridging session whose old callback fires late, resuming the new continuation if the callback closure references shared state. (c) The 20 s withTimeout cancels the coroutine; with suspendCoroutine it does not cancel anything, the SDK still reports later... but a late resume on a plain suspendCoroutine continuation after the coroutine already moved on cannot throw "Already resumed" unless it was previously resumed; so timeout alone does not explain it. (d) A coroutines library bug (unlikely: the message comes from the continuation state, not the dispatcher).
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with a fake SDK that fires success then failure; read the vendor changelog and ask their support; add logging with a per-session id on every callback; compare crash rate vs SDK version in Crashlytics custom keys; check logs for repeated onSuccess ids.
  5. Root cause: SDK 4.3 delivers terminal callbacks more than once; the bridge assumes exactly-once. suspendCoroutine throws IllegalStateException("Already resumed") on the second terminal call, on the vendor's thread, crashing the process (their thread has no handler). Using suspendCancellableCoroutine alone would not fix it if the first resume completed normally (second resume still throws), though it would absorb a resume after cancellation.
  6. Fix:
suspend fun IdvSdk.verify(doc: Doc): Verdict =
    suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
        val done = AtomicBoolean(false)
        val session = start(doc, object : IdvCallback {
            override fun onSuccess(v: Verdict) {
                if (done.compareAndSet(false, true)) cont.resume(v) { _, _, _ -> /* nothing to release */ }
            }
            override fun onFailure(e: IdvError) {
                if (done.compareAndSet(false, true)) cont.resumeWithException(e.toException())
                else log.w("IDV: late failure after terminal callback: $e")
            }
        })
        cont.invokeOnCancellation { session.cancel() }
    }

Short term: this guard plus the vendor ticket. Long term: model the SDK as a state machine in the adapter, with the first terminal result winning, and expose retries as new sessions only. 7. Prevention: Contract tests that run the adapter against a fake SDK firing {success,failure}, {failure,success}, {success,success}, and late-after-cancel, asserting no crash and first-wins; enforce "every bridge has an AtomicBoolean or documents exactly-once"; staged rollout with crash-rate guardrails per SDK version. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not try/catch (IllegalStateException) around resume (it hides other bugs and the thread is the vendor's). Not isActive checks as the guard (race). First-wins may hide a legitimately better late result; if the vendor says the late failure should override, handle that in domain logic with the log as evidence.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if success and failure race on two threads? → The compareAndSet makes exactly one win; the loser is dropped and logged.
  • What if the SDK fires success twice with different verdicts? → First wins; raise with the vendor; if the second is authoritative, the adapter must buffer until a vendor "final" marker.
  • What about callbackFlow instead? → Not needed; it is one-shot. A flow would force callers to deal with extra emissions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a payment SDK emitted onComplete on UI-triggered cancel after already delivering onSuccess. The crash appeared only for users with flaky networks and only after the vendor's patch release; the guard shipped within a day, but the real fix was a contract test suite the vendor's releases had to pass in CI before we bumped the dependency.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Wraps resume in try/catch or just swaps the builder.
  • Hire: Identifies exactly-once violation, adds atomic guard, keeps cancellation handling.
  • Strong hire: Explains which thread dies and why, adds contract tests with orderings, handles vendor escalation and staged rollout guardrails.

questions.promptHtml: A callback fires on an arbitrary SDK thread, at an unpredictable rate. Inside callbackFlow, how do you choose between send, trySend and trySendBlocking, and how do you choose the buffer? What can you lose, and what can you break?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who copy the snippet from those who understand that a callback is not a suspend context and a buffer policy is a data-loss decision.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Callbacks are plain functions on someone else's thread, so I can't use suspending send. trySend never blocks and never throws; it returns a ChannelResult that I may check. With the default BUFFERED capacity (64, suspend on overflow) a slow collector makes trySend fail once full, so events are dropped silently unless I look at the result. So the buffer policy is the real decision: conflate() when only the latest matters (location, battery), buffer(UNLIMITED) only when every event matters and rate is bounded, DROP_OLDEST/DROP_LATEST with a size when I want a window. trySendBlocking blocks the SDK's thread until there is room, so I only use it when that thread is mine and a stall is acceptable; never on Main or a sensor thread."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
callbackFlow's ProducerScope is a SendChannel. Its three send APIs:

API Suspends? Blocks thread? On full buffer (SUSPEND policy) On closed channel
send yes (needs coroutine) no suspends throws
trySend no no returns failure returns closed failure, no throw
trySendBlocking no yes (runBlocking-like) blocks until space returns closed failure

The default for callbackFlow is Channel.BUFFERED = 64 (can be changed globally by the system property kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer), onBufferOverflow = SUSPEND. With SUSPEND, trySend onto a full buffer fails (that is how trySend communicates "would suspend"). Operators applied right after the builder (buffer(n, overflow), conflate()) fuse and replace the builder's channel config rather than adding a second queue:

callbackFlow {...}.conflate()          -> one CONFLATED channel     (keeps latest)
callbackFlow {...}.buffer(UNLIMITED)   -> one UNLIMITED channel     (never loses, can OOM)
callbackFlow {...}.buffer(8, DROP_OLDEST) -> window of newest 8
callbackFlow {...}                     -> 64, SUSPEND: trySend fails when full => silent loss

Ordering: a channel is FIFO and trySend is thread-safe; events from one thread are ordered; events from multiple SDK threads are ordered by the order trySend wins, which may differ from SDK emission order if the SDK itself delivers concurrently.

Threading corollaries:

  • The code in the callback runs on the SDK thread; keep it to trySend. Do not do mapping, I/O or locks that the SDK thread depends on.
  • The collector side runs in the collector's context. Use flowOn to move the upstream mapping off the collector's thread (details in the flowOn chunk); the callback itself remains on the SDK thread regardless.
  • trySendBlocking on the main looper thread blocks UI: it is an ANR vector when the collector is slow. On a dedicated HandlerThread it simply applies backpressure to your own thread.
  • Never use runBlocking { send(x) } in a callback; same problem with extra overhead.

Making loss visible: trySend(x).onFailure { dropped.incrementAndGet() }, or .isFailure metrics. A silently dropping bridge is the worst of both worlds.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun Bus.events(): Flow<Event> = callbackFlow {
    val l = Listener { e ->
        val r = trySend(e)
        if (r.isFailure && !r.isClosed) metrics.droppedEvents.inc()   // full buffer, not shutdown
    }
    subscribe(l)
    awaitClose { unsubscribe(l) }
}.buffer(capacity = 256, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming the default is unlimited and nothing is lost.
  • buffer(UNLIMITED) on a firehose with a stalled collector (memory growth until OOM).
  • Using trySendBlocking on the SDK's single delivery thread, stalling every other listener of that SDK.
  • Ignoring the closed-vs-full distinction when logging failures.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does trySend not throw when the channel is closed? → Because callbacks routinely race with cancellation; throwing would crash SDK threads.
  2. When is UNLIMITED right? → Low-rate, must-not-lose events (payments, messages) with a bounded producer, and ideally persisted soon after.
  3. How would you guarantee no loss with a high rate? → Persist to disk (Room/queue) in the callback or via a dedicated consumer thread, then stream from the DB; the Flow is only the notification.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use trySend." Senior frames the buffer as a loss policy, knows the 64 default and fusion, instruments drops, and refuses to block foreign threads.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A telemetry stream used default buffering and silently dropped about 3% of events under load; no crash, just incomplete data until drop counters were added.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (2M DAU) has a feed that does Call.await() through a custom OkHttp extension for non-Retrofit endpoints. After a redesign with fast swipe-through of categories, data usage per session rose 38%, server QPS from this client is 2.2x higher than product expected, and the p95 of the feed endpoint is 2.4 s on slow networks. Also viewModelScope children survive after leaving the screen, LeakCanary reports FeedFragment retained for up to 30 s (the OkHttp read timeout).

suspend fun Call.await(): Response = suspendCoroutine { cont ->
    enqueue(object : Callback {
        override fun onResponse(call: Call, response: Response) = cont.resume(response)
        override fun onFailure(call: Call, e: IOException) = cont.resumeWithException(e)
    })
}

fun load(category: String) {
    job?.cancel()
    job = viewModelScope.launch {
        val body = client.newCall(req(category)).await().body!!.string()
        _state.value = parse(body)
    }
}

Red herrings: "the server is slow", "swipes cause duplicate triggers from the UI".
questions.promptHtml: The job?.cancel() is there, so why is old work still happening? Diagnose, fix, and prove the improvement.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds debounce to swipes or caches responses, treating the symptom. Or says "cancel() should stop it" without understanding why it does not.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do cancelled requests show in server logs as completed (yes: 2.2x QPS)? Is the bridge suspendCoroutine or cancellable (I'd read the code)? Are responses closed? Dispatcher maxRequestsPerHost (default 5) saturation: are new requests queued behind zombie ones?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: switch the bridge to suspendCancellableCoroutine with invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }: a ten-line change; roll out via staged release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The bridge is non-cancellable: job.cancel() marks the Job cancelled but the coroutine is parked in suspendCoroutine, the OkHttp call continues, and its callback resumes later; (b) because OkHttp's dispatcher runs max 5 concurrent requests per host, zombies block the new requests (explains p95); (c) captured this/ViewModel/Fragment references keep the retained objects until the call times out; (d) UI duplicate triggers (red herring: the log shows one load per swipe).
  4. How I'd verify each: OkHttp EventListener logging callStart/callEnd/canceled per call; compare counts with and without the fix; Android Studio Network Inspector; LeakCanary leak trace showing the Continuation; client.dispatcher.runningCallsCount() logging; server-side access logs for client-aborted connections.
  5. Root cause: suspendCoroutine provides a Continuation unaware of the Job. Cancelling the parent Job does not resume the suspended coroutine, and nothing calls Call.cancel(). The request runs to completion or timeout, wasting data and dispatcher slots. After it finishes, the response resumes the coroutine and it hits cancellation at the next suspension point, but only then. Meanwhile the callback closure retains everything it captures.
  6. Fix:
suspend fun Call.await(): Response = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }                           // aborts the socket
    enqueue(object : Callback {
        override fun onResponse(call: Call, response: Response) {
            cont.resume(response) { _, r, _ -> r.close() }           // cancelled before delivery: free the body
        }
        override fun onFailure(call: Call, e: IOException) {
            if (!cont.isCancelled) cont.resumeWithException(e)       // cancel() causes IOException("Canceled"); ignore noise
        }
    })
}

Plus response.use { ... } at the call site (the original also leaks response bodies). Long-term: prefer Retrofit suspend or OkHttp's own coroutine support if available in your version, rather than owning a bridge; add a debug check that cancelled calls reach callEnd quickly. 7. Prevention: A test using MockWebServer with a delayed response: launch, cancel after 100 ms, assert the server sees the connection closed and call.isCanceled. EventListener metrics for "cancelled calls" in production. Review rule: no suspendCoroutine in code review. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not extra debouncing as the fix. Not shorter timeouts (breaks slow networks). Cancelling a request is not always safe server-side for non-idempotent calls; here GETs only. Not GlobalScope to "let it finish and cache".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the request is a POST? → Cancelling may or may not have been processed by the server; use idempotency keys and treat result as unknown.
  • What if you want cancelled responses to still populate the cache? → Decouple: a separate scope that finishes and caches, deliberately; that is a product decision.
  • How do you prove the fix? → Compare QPS and bytes per session in a staged A/B: expect QPS to drop to near the user-intent count.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from an image-heavy feed: after the fix, bytes per session dropped by a third and the p95 dropped because new requests no longer queued behind five zombie calls to the same host. The cost savings on CDN egress paid for the engineer-week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds debounce/caching; thinks cancel() always stops work.
  • Hire: Finds the non-cancellable bridge, fixes with suspendCancellableCoroutine and Call.cancel().
  • Strong hire: Adds dispatcher-slot explanation, body closing via onCancellation, MockWebServer cancellation test, and POST/idempotency caveat with measurable verification.

questions.promptHtml: In a bridge, how should errors flow? Compare close(cause), cancel(CancellationException(...)), resumeWithException, and exceptions thrown from inside callbacks or from the registration call.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Error semantics in bridges are where cancellation and failure get confused, and where SDK threads crash. Seniors must keep the distinction and protect the SDK thread.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "For one-shot bridges: resumeWithException for failures; the caller sees the real exception. For callbackFlow: close(cause) terminates the flow with that exception, which the collector or catch sees as a normal failure. cancel(CancellationException(...)) is cancellation, not failure: it ends the producer and downstream sees a CancellationException, which in many structures just silently stops the collector's coroutine, so I avoid it for real errors even though the official example uses it. I never throw from inside an SDK callback, because the exception lands on the SDK's thread and can kill the process. And if the registration call itself throws, I let it propagate as a flow exception or close(e) so the collector can handle it."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Four exits, four meanings:

suspend bridge:
  resume(v)                         -> caller gets v
  resumeWithException(e)            -> caller gets e thrown (catchable)
  coroutine cancelled               -> caller gets CancellationException (not an error)

callbackFlow:
  trySend(x)                        -> element
  close()                           -> normal completion
  close(e)                          -> completes with e: collector's catch {} sees e
  cancel(CancellationException(..)) -> producer cancelled: downstream sees CancellationException
                                       => treated as cancellation, not failure
  block throws                      -> propagates to collector as failure

Why close(e) over cancel for errors: exception transparency means catch handles real exceptions, while a CancellationException thrown while the collector's own Job is active is generally treated as "this coroutine was cancelled", so catch does not turn it into a UI state and a plain launch {} ends silently. If you use the doc's cancel(CancellationException("API Error", cause)) pattern, test what your downstream does with it. Reserve cancel for "I was told to stop".

Thrown exceptions in callbacks: the callback runs on the SDK's thread, outside any coroutine. Anything thrown (for example from your own parsing code or from resume on a completed continuation) goes to the SDK's thread handler or the default uncaught handler. So: callbacks should do only trySend, resume*, close, all non-throwing in the normal path (aside from double resume). Map exceptions to domain types before sending (sealed class Update { data class Value; data class Failure }) if failure is not terminal.

Registration failures: an exception from register inside the suspendCancellableCoroutine block propagates directly out of the call to the caller (it is a normal call in the caller's stack). In callbackFlow it propagates through the flow. If something is half registered, clean up before rethrowing (try { register() } catch (e: Throwable) { unregister(); throw e }).

CancellationException as data: never resumeWithException(CancellationException()) for a failure; the coroutine would appear cancelled. Convert SDK "user cancelled" into a domain result (sealed class Outcome { object UserCancelled }) because from the app's point of view that is a normal outcome.

Non-terminal errors (transient disconnect in a sensor/socket) are better modelled in the stream: Flow<Result<T>> or a sealed state, with the flow staying alive. Terminal errors close it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface Reading { data class Value(val v: Float) : Reading; data class Glitch(val code: Int) : Reading }

fun Sdk.readings(): Flow<Reading> = callbackFlow {
    val l = object : SdkListener {
        override fun onValue(v: Float) { trySend(Reading.Value(v)) }
        override fun onTransient(code: Int) { trySend(Reading.Glitch(code)) }   // non-terminal
        override fun onFatal(e: SdkException) { close(e) }                      // terminal failure
        override fun onUserCancelled() { close() }                              // normal completion
    }
    try {
        register(l)
    } catch (t: Throwable) {
        unregister(l)       // half-registered: clean up, then fail the flow
        throw t
    }
    awaitClose { unregister(l) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using cancel(...) for errors, then wondering why catch never fires and the screen shows nothing.
  • resumeWithException(CancellationException) for SDK errors.
  • Throwing from callback code on SDK threads.
  • Catching Throwable around resume instead of fixing the double-fire.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens when close(e) is called twice? → The channel is already closed; the second call returns false and does nothing.
  2. Where does an exception from trySend get thrown? → It does not throw; it returns a result.
  3. Should an SDK cancelled callback end the flow? → If it's a user action, usually close() or a sentinel domain value; the caller decides if it is an error.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use close(e) or resumeWithException." Senior defends the cancel-vs-failure distinction, protects SDK threads, models non-terminal errors in the data, and cleans up partial registration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A scanner SDK threw a parse exception from inside its callback chain; the vendor thread had no handler and the process died with a stack that never mentioned the app's code.

questions.contextHtml: A health-device app (350k MAU, BLE glucose meters) uses a vendor SDK with this callback API: connect(device, ConnectionCb), readHistory(range, ResultCb), startLiveStream(StreamCb), disconnect(). Rules from the vendor docs: only one operation at a time per device, connect can take up to 45 s, disconnect() must be called after any aborted operation or the next connect fails with BUSY, and StreamCb.onReading fires up to 10 times per second until stopLiveStream(). Today the app uses nested callbacks in the ViewModel; users report "stuck on connecting" and rare BUSY errors after leaving the screen mid-sync (about 4% of syncs). Product wants a 20 s cap on connect with a retry, cancel-on-leave, and a live graph.
questions.promptHtml: Design the coroutine-based wrapper. How do you model each operation, handle cancellation and timeouts so the device is never left in a bad state, and enforce one-operation-at-a-time?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Wraps each callback in suspendCoroutine and calls withTimeout. Ignores that cancel/timeouts must call disconnect, that operations may overlap, and that the live stream is multi-shot.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the SDK thread-safe, and which thread does it call back on? Is disconnect() idempotent and safe in any state? Does an aborted readHistory leave partial data? Can two screens use the device (one owner)? Is battery/radio use a concern for the live stream?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (4% BUSY) Ensure disconnect() always runs on leaving the screen via a single cleanup path, even before the redesign.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (for the BUSY/stuck state): (a) leave-screen abort does not call disconnect; (b) two operations overlap (retry tapped while connecting); (c) callback after screen death mutates stale state; (d) connect waits 45 s with no user-visible timeout.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add structured logging with an operation id; a fake SDK with scripted delays/failures in tests; reproduce "leave mid-sync" with an instrumented test; collect BUSY rates by app state.
  5. Root cause: Operations are not tied to the lifecycle of the caller, and the device state machine is not protected: cancellation and timeouts are not reflected into SDK-level cleanup.
  6. Fix / design:
  • One-shot operations become cancellable suspend functions whose cancellation aborts the device state:
class DeviceClient(private val sdk: Sdk, private val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    private val gate = Mutex()                                  // one operation at a time

    suspend fun <T> op(block: suspend () -> T): T = gate.withLock {
        try { block() } catch (e: Throwable) { withContext(NonCancellable) { sdk.disconnect() }; throw e }
    }

    suspend fun connect(d: Device): Unit = op {
        withTimeout(20_000) {                                    // timeout cancels the continuation
            suspendCancellableCoroutine { c ->
                val h = sdk.connect(d, object : ConnectionCb {
                    override fun onConnected() = c.resume(Unit)
                    override fun onError(e: SdkError) = c.resumeWithException(e.asException())
                })
                c.invokeOnCancellation { h.abort() }             // fast, non-blocking
            }
        }
    }

    fun live(): Flow<Reading> = callbackFlow {
        val cb = StreamCb { r -> trySend(r) }
        sdk.startLiveStream(cb)
        awaitClose { sdk.stopLiveStream(cb) }
    }.conflate()                                                 // graph needs the latest, not all
}
  • Retry policy in the caller: retry(2) { connect(d) } with backoff, where timeouts are a failure (TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException subclass; convert it at the boundary with withTimeoutOrNull or catch carefully so a timeout does not look like the caller being cancelled).
  • The Mutex makes connect, readHistory and a live stream's lifetime mutually exclusive; if the stream must coexist with other commands, model the device as an actor with a command channel instead (see the shared-state chunk for Mutex vs actor trade-offs).
  • Scope ownership: the client is app-scoped but each operation runs in the caller's scope, so leaving the screen cancels the call, which triggers disconnect().
  • A caveat: Mutex is not reentrant. op {} inside op {} deadlocks, so compose at the top level.
  1. Prevention: Fake SDK tests for: cancel mid-connect -> disconnect called once; timeout -> BUSY never occurs on next connect; overlapping calls serialize; stream cancel -> stopLiveStream. Metrics: connect duration p95, BUSY rate, timeouts.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not GlobalScope for sync (can't cancel on leave). Not infinite retries. Not putting disconnect() in invokeOnCancellation (can block); use the post-cancel NonCancellable path or a non-blocking abort(). Serialization limits throughput; acceptable because the device itself is serial.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if abort() is itself asynchronous and connect must not start before it finishes? → Make the gate's cleanup await a completion callback (another bridge) before releasing the Mutex.
  • What if the live stream must continue in the background? → That is a foreground-service decision; the wrapper stays the same but the collector lives in the service's scope.
  • How would you test the timeout? → runTest with virtual time and a fake SDK that never calls back; advance 20 s and assert failure and cleanup.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: after the rewrite, "stuck on connecting" disappeared because timeouts finally mapped to abort() and disconnect(); the remaining BUSY cases came from a second screen holding the device, solved by making the client the single owner.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suspendCoroutine with withTimeout, no cleanup path.
  • Hire: Cancellable bridges, timeouts with abort, callbackFlow with stop, serialization.
  • Strong hire: Separates abort from disconnect, handles NonCancellable cleanup, addresses timeout-as-cancellation semantics, Mutex re-entrancy, actor alternative, and deterministic tests with virtual time.

questions.contextHtml: The team must expose a legacy in-house NetworkMonitor as a Flow. Its API: setListener(l: Listener?). Only one listener at a time: setting a new one silently replaces the old, setListener(null) clears it. Three features want connectivity: the offline banner (lives while the app is foreground), the upload queue (lives while uploads are pending, may overlap the banner), and analytics (lives always). The product spec says only "expose connectivity as a Flow so any feature can observe it". After a first attempt with a callbackFlow per consumer, QA reports "the banner stops updating after an upload starts" and "analytics goes silent after visiting settings" (reproducible 100%).
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with the straightforward approach, what questions do you ask about the unclear requirement, and how do you design it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames lifecycle timing or race conditions; adds delay between collections. Or makes the monitor a global MutableSharedFlow set up at startup without thinking about when it should stop.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I change NetworkMonitor (or wrap it)? Must connectivity stop being monitored when nobody is interested (battery) or is it cheap? Do consumers need the current value immediately (state) or only changes? Can the banner and analytics tolerate a conflated latest value? Who owns the process-level scope?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the symptom stop by having exactly one registration: temporarily register one app-lifetime listener feeding a MutableStateFlow, which consumers read.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Each callbackFlow calls setListener(mine), replacing the previous consumer's listener; (b) an earlier consumer's awaitClose calls setListener(null), clearing a newer consumer's listener; (c) lifecycle ordering of collectors; (d) dispatcher issue. (a) and (b) match "banner stops after upload starts" and "analytics silent after visiting settings".
  4. How I'd verify each: A fake monitor that records setListener calls and the current listener identity; a test collecting two flows and cancelling one; logs of listener identity transitions.
  5. Root cause: The cold-per-collector model assumes registrations are additive. This API is exclusive: the registration is a shared mutable resource, so the Flow wrapper must be a single upstream shared by consumers, with a reference-counted lifetime. The cleanup bug (b) is the standard compare-and-clear mistake: unregistering by null rather than "only if still mine".
  6. Fix:
class ConnectivityRepo(private val monitor: NetworkMonitor, scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val upstream: Flow<Boolean> = callbackFlow {
        val l = Listener { online -> trySend(online) }
        monitor.setListener(l)
        trySend(monitor.isOnline())                      // seed with current state
        awaitClose { if (monitor.currentListener() === l) monitor.setListener(null) }   // clear only if still ours
    }.distinctUntilChanged()

    val online: StateFlow<Boolean> =
        upstream.stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), monitor.isOnline())
}

All three features collect repo.online; exactly one underlying registration exists while at least one collector is active, and it is removed 5 s after the last disappears. If the SDK exposes no currentListener(), track ownership inside the repository (an AtomicReference), because the repository is now the only code allowed to call setListener. Short term: the shared repository. Long term: delete the public setListener or replace it with an additive addListener API. 7. Prevention: Make the exclusive resource private to one class; unit test "two collectors, one cancels, other keeps receiving"; document in the wrapper that the underlying API is exclusive; lint/review rule against calling setListener outside the wrapper. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not one callbackFlow per feature. Not SharingStarted.Eagerly for the process lifetime if battery matters (analytics can accept a stale gap if it uses WhileSubscribed; if analytics must not miss a transition, give it its own always-on consumer that keeps the sharing active). Not delaying collection to dodge ordering issues. stateIn conflates, so features that need every transition (rare here) need a different design. The sharing operators are covered in their own chunk; here I am pointing out why interop forces them.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if another team still calls setListener directly? → Wrapping cannot protect against that; enforce through visibility (internal) and review, or fix the SDK to be additive.
  • What if the initial value is unknown until the first callback? → Use StateFlow<Connectivity?> or a sealed Unknown/Online/Offline rather than faking false.
  • What if you must support a library that is also internally replacing the listener? → Wrap the library once at the lowest layer and expose only the shared stream upward.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a legacy analytics SDK's setCallback had been silently replaced by a feature module for two releases; metrics for a whole funnel step were missing until someone traced listener ownership. The fix was a single owner with a shared flow, and a test that fails if anything else touches the setter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Treats it as a timing bug; per-consumer callbackFlow remains.
  • Hire: Identifies exclusive-listener semantics, centralises registration, shares upstream.
  • Strong hire: Adds compare-and-clear cleanup, seeds initial state, chooses sharing/stop policy with battery reasoning, and asks about the SDK ownership and delivery requirements before coding.
